The median lies between the mode and mean in a skewed distribution; it is not the lowest.
Rationale: Skew is named for the tail. When scores bunch at the low end with a tail to the right, the distribution is positively skewed, and the mean (most sensitive to extreme scores) is pulled toward the tail: mode < median < mean. In a negative skew the order reverses. The median is often preferred for describing skewed data.
References: Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Descriptive statistics: skewness and measures of central tendency
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

111. nce-s-ass-039 · Research and Program Evaluation · correlation and shared variance · medium · In review

In a clinic sample, weekly exercise hours correlate -.70 with depression scores, and nightly hours of sleep correlate +.40 with depression scores. Which conclusion is accurate?
A. The sleep link is stronger because its coefficient is positive
The sign shows direction only; strength depends on the absolute value, and .70 exceeds .40.
B. Exercise accounts for 70% of the variance in depression scores
Shared variance is r squared, so -.70 corresponds to 49%, not 70%.
C. The negative coefficient shows exercise reduces depression
Correlation does not establish causation; a third variable or reverse direction could explain it.
D. The exercise link is stronger and shares 49% of the variance ✔ KEY
The absolute value .70 is larger than .40, and r squared (.49) gives the proportion of shared variance.
Rationale: A correlation coefficient's sign gives direction and its absolute value gives strength. Squaring r gives the coefficient of determination, the proportion of variance the two variables share. No correlation, however strong, demonstrates cause and effect.
References: Erford (Research and Evaluation in Counseling) — Correlation: direction, strength, and coefficient of determination
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

112. nce-s-ass-040 · Assessment and Testing · screening instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, AUDIT, CAGE) · medium · In review

An elementary school principal proposes using scores from a 10-minute behavior screening checklist, completed once by each teacher, to decide which students are placed in special education services. What is the school counselor's BEST advice?
A. Accept the plan if the checklist has internal consistency above .80
Good reliability does not make a brief screener valid for a high-stakes placement decision.
B. Use the screener to flag students for a full multi-measure evaluation ✔ KEY
Screeners identify who needs further assessment; high-stakes decisions require comprehensive evaluation from multiple sources.
C. Raise the cutoff score so that fewer students are wrongly identified
Changing the cutoff trades false positives for false negatives and still leaves a single screener driving placement.
D. Keep the screener but have a second teacher rescore every checklist
Double scoring reduces clerical error but does not address the misuse of a screener for a high-stakes decision.
Rationale: Screening instruments are brief and built to cast a wide net, accepting some false positives. High-stakes decisions such as placement, diagnosis, or eligibility should rest on multiple measures, multiple informants, and qualified professional judgment rather than a single score.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Screening versus comprehensive assessment; high-stakes testing
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

113. nce-s-ass-041 · Assessment and Testing · screening instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, AUDIT, CAGE) · easy · In review

A counselor at a university counseling center plans to give the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) to new clients. Which description of the BDI-II is accurate?
A. A 21-item self-report of depressive symptoms over two weeks ✔ KEY
The BDI-II is a 21-item self-report of depressive symptom severity covering the past two weeks, including today.
B. A clinician-administered interview that yields DSM-5-TR diagnoses
The BDI-II is a self-report severity measure, not a diagnostic interview.
C. A projective technique that uncovers depressive themes in children
It is an objective self-report inventory, and it is intended for adolescents and adults.
D. A nine-item primary care screen keyed to DSM depression criteria
That describes the PHQ-9; the BDI-II has 21 items and was developed separately from primary care screening.
Rationale: The BDI-II measures the severity of depressive symptoms in adolescents and adults, with each item rated 0 to 3. It is useful for screening and tracking change but does not by itself establish a diagnosis; a clinical interview is still needed.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Assessment of depression: Beck Depression Inventory-II
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

114. nce-s-ass-042 · Assessment and Testing · personality inventories (MMPI-3, NEO-PI) · hard · In review

On an MMPI-3 completed during a disability evaluation, the inconsistent-responding scales are within normal limits, but the infrequent-responding (overreporting) scales are markedly elevated, as are many clinical scales. What is the MOST appropriate interpretation?
A. Random responding, so the client probably could not read the items
Normal inconsistency scales argue against random or content-unrelated responding.
B. Defensive underreporting, so true problems are likely even more severe
Underreporting is shown by the underreporting scales, not by elevated infrequent-responding scales.
C. A valid profile, so the elevations confirm severe psychopathology
Marked elevations on overreporting scales call the validity of substantive scale scores into question.
D. Possible overreporting, so the clinical scales need cautious reading ✔ KEY
Elevated infrequent-responding scales with consistent responding suggest symptom overreporting, which limits face-value interpretation.
Rationale: MMPI-3 validity scales fall into three groups: inconsistent responding (CRIN, VRIN, TRIN), overreporting (F, Fp, Fs, FBS, RBS), and underreporting (L, K). The validity scales are reviewed before any substantive scale. When overreporting indicators are markedly elevated, substantive elevations may reflect exaggeration rather than true symptoms, particularly in settings with external incentives.
References: Hays (Assessment) — MMPI-3 validity scales: inconsistency, overreporting, underreporting
⚑ Check: Verify the MMPI-3 validity scale names and groupings listed in the rationale against the current manual.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

115. nce-s-ass-043 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · intake interview structure · medium · In review

A counselor uses the SCID-5 at intake. It follows a set order of questions keyed to DSM-5 criteria but lets the counselor ask follow-up questions and use clinical judgment in rating each criterion. How is this interview format BEST classified?
A. Fully structured, read word for word with no clinical judgment
Fully structured interviews (often designed for lay interviewers) leave no room for follow-up probes or clinician judgment.
B. Unstructured, with topics guided mainly by the client's story
Unstructured interviews have no set question sequence, unlike the SCID-5.
C. Semi-structured, a set guide with room for clinician probes ✔ KEY
The SCID-5 is a semi-structured interview: standard questions plus clinician follow-up and judgment.
D. A mental status exam, since it records observed presentation
An MSE describes current presentation; the SCID-5 is a diagnostic interview organized by DSM criteria.
Rationale: Structured interviews maximize reliability and coverage but limit flexibility; unstructured interviews maximize flexibility and rapport but are less reliable and can miss areas. Semi-structured interviews such as the SCID-5 combine a standard framework with clinician probes, balancing reliability and clinical depth.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Clinical interviews: structured, semi-structured, and unstructured
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

116. nce-s-ass-044 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · mental status examination · easy · In review

Asked how she has been feeling, a 40-year-old client says, "Honestly, I'm good, really good." Throughout the interview she is tearful, her voice trembles, and her facial expression changes little. How should the counselor document this in the mental status examination?
A. Mood as the observed tears; affect as her statement of "good"
This reverses the terms: mood is self-reported, affect is observed.
B. Mood reported as "good"; affect tearful and mood-incongruent ✔ KEY
Mood is the client's stated emotional state; affect is the counselor's observation, here incongruent with the stated mood.
C. Thought content as denial; thought process as tearful and flat
Tearfulness is an affect finding, and thought process describes how ideas connect, not emotional expression.
D. Insight as intact, because she can describe how she is feeling
Her report conflicts with her presentation, so this does not show intact insight into her condition.
Rationale: In the MSE, mood is the sustained emotion the client reports (often quoted), and affect is the observed expression of emotion, described by range, intensity, stability, and congruence with mood and content. Thought process is how thoughts connect; thought content is what the client thinks about; insight and judgment are rated separately.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Mental status examination: mood and affect
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

117. nce-s-ass-045 · Assessment and Testing · collateral information and records · medium · In review

A 9-year-old is referred for inattention and angry outbursts. On a behavior rating scale, the parent's ratings are highly elevated, the teacher's ratings are in the average range, and the child's self-report is low. How should the counselor interpret these results?
A. Informant differences are common and show where problems appear ✔ KEY
Discrepancies often reflect real differences across settings and relationships, and they guide further assessment.
B. The teacher's ratings are most objective, so set the parent's aside
No single informant is automatically correct; discarding the parent data loses information about home behavior.
C. Self-reports from children this age are invalid and add nothing
Children can provide useful information, especially about internal states, when measures fit their age.
D. The gap shows the parent is exaggerating, so assessment can end
The discrepancy is a reason to explore further, not evidence of exaggeration or a reason to stop.
Rationale: Assessment of children and adolescents relies on multiple informants (parents, teachers, the youth) and multiple methods, as in the Achenbach System of Empirically Based Assessment. Low cross-informant agreement is typical, because behavior varies by setting and each rater sees a different slice. Counselors integrate the reports with observation and history rather than choosing one.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Assessing children: multiple informants and settings
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

118. nce-s-ass-046 · Assessment and Testing · DSM-5-TR diagnostic structure and specifiers · hard · In review

For the past four weeks, a 33-year-old client has had depressed mood and two other depressive symptoms, causing clear impairment at work. There is no identifiable stressor, and no other mental disorder or medical cause explains the symptoms. The counselor wants the record to state why full criteria are not met. Which diagnosis BEST fits?
A. Unspecified depressive disorder, because no full criteria are met
Unspecified is used when the clinician chooses not to give the reason or lacks the information; here the counselor wants to state it.
B. Major depressive disorder, single episode, mild in severity
A major depressive episode requires at least five symptoms; this client has three.
C. Adjustment disorder with depressed mood, given the impairment
Adjustment disorder requires an identifiable stressor, which is absent.
D. Other specified depressive disorder, noting the specific reason ✔ KEY
Other specified is used when the clinician records the reason the presentation falls short, such as insufficient symptoms.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR offers two options for presentations that cause distress or impairment but do not meet full criteria for a disorder in a class. "Other specified" is used when the clinician chooses to communicate the specific reason (for example, a depressive episode with insufficient symptoms). "Unspecified" is used when the clinician chooses not to specify the reason, including when there is not enough information, as in an emergency setting.
References: DSM-5-TR — Use of other specified and unspecified disorders; Other Specified Depressive Disorder
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

119. nce-s-ass-047 · Social and Cultural Diversity · culturally fair assessment · easy · In review

A counselor is seeing a 38-year-old client who recently immigrated and describes her distress mainly in terms of family duty and spiritual concerns. The counselor wants a DSM-5-TR tool that explores the client's own explanation of the problem, cultural identity, sources of support, and expectations of help. Which tool should the counselor use?
A. Level 1 Cross-Cutting Symptom Measure
This measure screens symptom domains; it does not explore cultural explanations or help-seeking.
B. WHO Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0
The WHODAS 2.0 assesses functioning and disability, not cultural understanding of the problem.
C. Cultural Formulation Interview ✔ KEY
The CFI asks about the cultural definition of the problem, perceived causes, cultural identity, stressors and supports, and help-seeking.
D. Structured Clinical Interview (SCID-5)
The SCID-5 is a diagnostic interview organized by criteria, not a cultural assessment.
Rationale: The DSM-5-TR Cultural Formulation Interview is a person-centered, semi-structured set of questions in Section III. It covers the cultural definition of the problem, cultural perceptions of cause, context, and support, cultural factors affecting coping and help-seeking, and current help-seeking expectations. Informant and supplementary modules extend it.
References: DSM-5-TR — Section III: Cultural Formulation Interview · Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Culturally sensitive assessment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

120. nce-s-ass-048 · Assessment and Testing · screening instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, AUDIT, CAGE) · medium · In review

A 76-year-old client's daughter reports that he has trouble finding words and has missed paying several bills. On a brief cognitive screen such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), he scores below the screening cutoff. What should the counselor do NEXT?
A. Diagnose a major neurocognitive disorder based on the score
A screening score cannot establish a neurocognitive diagnosis or its cause.
B. Refer for a full medical and neuropsychological evaluation ✔ KEY
A positive screen calls for comprehensive evaluation to clarify the cause, including reversible conditions.
C. Readminister the same screen next week to confirm the result
Repeating the screen delays evaluation and adds practice effects without clarifying the cause.
D. Reassure the family that these changes reflect normal aging
Word-finding problems and new difficulty with finances go beyond expected age-related change and need evaluation.
Rationale: Cognitive screens such as the MoCA or MMSE flag possible impairment but are influenced by education, language, hearing, vision, and mood. A positive screen in an older adult should prompt medical evaluation (to rule out causes such as medication effects, thyroid problems, delirium, or depression) and fuller neuropsychological testing before any diagnosis is made.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Assessment of older adults: cognitive screening · DSM-5-TR — Neurocognitive disorders: major and mild NCD
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

121. nce-s-ass-049 · Human Growth and Development · differential diagnosis · medium · In review

An 8-year-old is referred for poor concentration, restlessness, and unfinished classwork. His teacher from last year describes him as attentive and settled. The problems began about five months ago, shortly after he witnessed a violent break-in at his home, and he now has nightmares and startles easily. Which finding MOST argues against ADHD as the primary explanation?
A. His restlessness is seen both at home and at school
Symptoms in two or more settings are required for ADHD, so this finding is consistent with ADHD rather than against it.
B. He is a boy referred in the early elementary years
Age and gender describe common referral patterns; they do not help separate ADHD from a trauma response.
C. The symptoms began suddenly after a traumatic event ✔ KEY
An abrupt onset after trauma, with no earlier history and with intrusion and arousal symptoms, points toward a trauma-related disorder.
D. His classwork is left unfinished, not done poorly
Failing to finish schoolwork is itself a listed ADHD inattention symptom, so it does not argue against ADHD.
Rationale: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder with a persistent pattern that typically shows up early and across settings. When attention problems and restlessness appear abruptly after a traumatic event in a child who was previously attentive, and they come with nightmares and an exaggerated startle response, a trauma- and stressor-related disorder better explains the picture. Hyperarousal and intrusive memories can look like inattention and hyperactivity, so onset timing and trauma history are key differentiators.
References: DSM-5-TR — Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: Differential Diagnosis · SAMHSA TIP 57 — Trauma-related symptoms that resemble other disorders
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

122. nce-s-ass-050 · Assessment and Testing · differential diagnosis · hard · In review

A 35-year-old client reports three weeks of depressed mood, loss of interest, guilt, and poor concentration. His partner says he has been "snappy and irritable" with everyone. He sleeps about four hours a night but wakes exhausted and drags through the day. He reports no past periods of elevated mood or unusual energy. Which diagnosis is BEST supported?
A. Major depressive disorder, single episode ✔ KEY
He has at least five depressive symptoms for two weeks or more; irritability and insomnia with fatigue fit a depressive episode.
B. Bipolar II disorder, current episode depressed
Bipolar II requires at least one past hypomanic episode, and he reports no periods of elevated mood or increased energy.
C. Cyclothymic disorder with depressive features
Cyclothymic disorder requires at least two years of fluctuating subthreshold symptoms, not a three-week episode.
D. Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder
DMDD is diagnosed only in children and adolescents (first diagnosis between ages 6 and 18), with onset before age 10.
Rationale: Irritability is common in depression and does not by itself suggest bipolarity. Hypomania requires a distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood together with increased activity or energy. This client sleeps little but feels exhausted, which is insomnia, not the decreased need for sleep seen in hypomania. With no history of hypomanic episodes, the depressive episode is best diagnosed as major depressive disorder.
References: DSM-5-TR — Major depressive disorder: Differential Diagnosis; hypomanic episode Criteria A-B
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

123. nce-s-ass-051 · Assessment and Testing · differential diagnosis · medium · In review

A 42-year-old client in a severe depressive episode believes she is being punished for terrible sins and that her organs are rotting. Her family reports that these beliefs appeared only after the depression began, and she has never had psychotic symptoms while her mood was stable. Which diagnosis BEST fits?
A. Schizophrenia, first episode, acute
Psychosis that occurs only during mood episodes points to a mood disorder; schizophrenia is excluded when mood episodes explain it.
B. Schizoaffective disorder, depressive type
Schizoaffective disorder requires delusions or hallucinations for two weeks or more without a major mood episode.
C. Delusional disorder, somatic type
Delusional disorder is not diagnosed when delusions occur only during major depressive or manic episodes.
D. MDD, severe, with psychotic features ✔ KEY
Delusions confined to a major depressive episode are coded with the psychotic features specifier.
Rationale: The deciding question is when the psychotic symptoms occur. If delusions or hallucinations happen only during a major depressive episode, the diagnosis is major depressive disorder with psychotic features; here the content (guilt, punishment, bodily decay) is mood-congruent. Schizoaffective disorder requires a period of at least two weeks of psychosis without a major mood episode, and schizophrenia is ruled out when mood episodes account for the psychosis.
References: DSM-5-TR — Depressive disorders: with psychotic features specifier; schizoaffective disorder Criterion B
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

124. nce-s-ass-052 · Assessment and Testing · differential diagnosis · hard · In review

A 24-year-old is brought in after four days of paranoid beliefs and hearing voices. He reports using methamphetamine daily for the past month and stopping two days ago. He has no prior psychiatric history. Which approach to diagnosis is MOST appropriate?
A. Diagnose schizophrenia, as he has delusions and hallucinations
Schizophrenia requires continuous signs for six months and is excluded when a substance explains the symptoms.
B. Consider a substance-induced psychosis and see if it clears ✔ KEY
Onset during heavy stimulant use suggests a substance-induced disorder; persistence well after stopping would point elsewhere.
C. Diagnose brief psychotic disorder, as it has lasted under a month
Brief psychotic disorder is not diagnosed when the disturbance is attributable to a substance.
D. Postpone any psychosis assessment until a 90-day program ends
Psychosis needs prompt assessment for safety and care; waiting months is not a diagnostic strategy.
Rationale: Stimulants such as methamphetamine can produce paranoia and hallucinations. DSM-5-TR asks whether the symptoms began during or soon after substance use and whether they persist for a substantial period (for example, about a month) after intoxication or withdrawal ends. Symptoms that clear with abstinence support a substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder; symptoms that persist, or a history of psychosis without use, suggest an independent psychotic disorder.
References: DSM-5-TR — Substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder: Criterion C and Differential Diagnosis
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

125. nce-s-ass-053 · Assessment and Testing · projective tests · easy · In review

A counselor gives a client a form with stems such as "I regret..." and "My father..." and asks her to finish each one in her own words. Which type of instrument is this?
A. A sentence completion test such as the Rotter ✔ KEY
Incomplete sentence stems that the client finishes freely define the sentence completion method, such as the Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank.
B. An objective personality inventory like the MMPI-3
The MMPI-3 uses fixed true/false items scored against scales, not open-ended responses.
C. A word association technique in the style of Jung
Word association asks for the first word that comes to mind after a single stimulus word, not completing sentences.
D. A symptom checklist such as the SCL-90-R measure
The SCL-90-R asks clients to rate how much listed symptoms have bothered them, a structured self-report format.
Rationale: Sentence completion tests are often called semi-structured projective techniques: the stem gives some structure, but the client supplies the content, which may reveal attitudes, conflicts, and concerns. The Rotter Incomplete Sentences Blank is the best-known example. Like other projectives, responses are interpreted with caution and alongside other data.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Projective personality assessment: sentence completion techniques
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

126. nce-s-ass-054 · Assessment and Testing · projective tests · medium · In review

As part of an evaluation for possible depression, a school counselor asks a 9-year-old to draw a house, a tree, and a person. Afterward, a colleague proposes diagnosing depression because the tree in the drawing has no leaves. Which response BEST reflects sound practice with this technique?
A. Accept the sign, as drawing tests are well validated for mood
Individual drawing signs have weak and inconsistent research support for diagnosing specific disorders.
B. Rescore the drawing with a longer and more detailed checklist
A longer checklist does not fix the underlying validity problem of reading diagnoses from single drawing features.
C. Treat the drawing as a hypothesis to check against other data ✔ KEY
Projective drawings are best used for rapport and hypothesis generation, confirmed by interviews, ratings, and other measures.
D. Have the child draw again and diagnose if the sign is repeated
Repeating the task does not make the sign a valid indicator of depression; the diagnosis still lacks evidence.
Rationale: The House-Tree-Person technique, developed by Buck, asks the client to draw and then talk about the drawings. Interpreting single features (such as a bare tree) as signs of a disorder has limited reliability and validity support. Projectives are best used to build rapport and generate hypotheses that are then checked against interview data, behavior ratings, collateral reports, and standardized measures.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Projective drawings (House-Tree-Person): uses and psychometric limitations
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

127. nce-s-ass-055 · Assessment and Testing · substance use assessment · medium · In review

Over the past year, a client's drinking has met these DSM-5-TR criteria: drinking more than intended, unsuccessful efforts to cut down, craving, continued use despite arguments with his spouse about it, and tolerance. He reports no withdrawal symptoms. Which severity specifier applies?
A. Mild, as no withdrawal symptoms are reported
Withdrawal is not required for any severity level; severity is set by how many criteria are met.
B. Moderate, based on the number of criteria met ✔ KEY
Five criteria fall in the moderate range (4-5 criteria); mild is 2-3 and severe is 6 or more.
C. Severe, as tolerance shows physical dependence
Tolerance is one criterion among eleven; it does not by itself raise the severity level.
D. Unspecified, until withdrawal is also confirmed
An alcohol use disorder can be diagnosed and rated without withdrawal; at least two criteria in 12 months are needed.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR substance use disorders have 11 criteria; at least two within a 12-month period are needed for the diagnosis. Severity is rated by count: mild (2-3 symptoms), moderate (4-5), and severe (6 or more). Physiological features such as tolerance and withdrawal are not required, and neither one alone determines severity.
References: DSM-5-TR — Alcohol use disorder: Criteria A and severity specifiers
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

128. nce-s-ass-056 · Assessment and Testing · substance use assessment · easy · In review

In an integrated primary care clinic, a 44-year-old patient screens positive on the AUDIT-C. What does this result BEST support as the next step?
A. Diagnosing alcohol use disorder, mild severity
A screening tool flags possible risk; it cannot establish whether DSM-5-TR criteria are met.
B. Referring the patient to inpatient detoxification
Level of care depends on a full assessment, such as of withdrawal risk, not on a positive screen alone.
C. Placing the patient in a relapse prevention group
Treatment placement before any diagnostic assessment skips the step that tells what care is needed.
D. Fuller assessment to see if a disorder exists ✔ KEY
A positive screen calls for further evaluation, such as the full AUDIT and a diagnostic interview.
Rationale: The AUDIT-C is the three consumption items of the 10-item AUDIT. Like all screeners, it is built to identify people who may have a problem, trading some precision for speed. A positive result is followed by a fuller assessment (for example, the complete AUDIT, a clinical interview against DSM-5-TR criteria, and review of consequences) before diagnosis or placement.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Substance use screening (AUDIT, AUDIT-C) versus diagnostic assessment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

129. nce-s-ass-057 · Assessment and Testing · substance use assessment · easy · In review

A counselor in a high school health center wants a brief substance use screening tool that was developed and validated specifically for adolescents. Which instrument BEST fits this need?
A. CRAFFT ✔ KEY
The CRAFFT was developed for adolescents and asks about situations such as riding in a car with an impaired driver.
B. CAGE questionnaire
The CAGE was developed for adults and focuses on lifetime alcohol problems, not adolescent use.
C. Michigan Alcoholism Screening Test
The MAST was developed with adults and screens for alcohol problems only.
D. Addiction Severity Index
The ASI is a longer adult interview measuring problem severity, not a brief adolescent screen.
Rationale: The CRAFFT is a brief screen for adolescent substance use risk. Its name comes from its key words: Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Friends, Trouble. It covers alcohol and other drugs and fits settings such as schools and pediatric care. Like any screen, a positive result leads to further assessment rather than diagnosis.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Substance use screening with adolescents: CRAFFT
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

130. nce-s-ass-058 · Human Growth and Development · biopsychosocial history · medium · In review

A parent brings a 6-year-old for an intake because of delayed speech and difficulty playing with peers. Which part of the biopsychosocial history is MOST important to gather in detail at this point?
A. The parent's own job history and career plans
Parent employment can matter for context, but it does not address the child's developmental concerns.
B. The child's scores on recent reading tests
At age 6, formal reading data are limited and do not explain early speech and social delays.
C. Developmental milestones and early health ✔ KEY
Timing of speech, motor, and social milestones, plus prenatal and early medical history, is central to these concerns.
D. The family's faith practices and affiliation
Spiritual context can be relevant to a full history, but it is not the priority for speech and social delays.
Rationale: For young children, the developmental history is a core section of the biopsychosocial assessment. When to first words, phrases, walking, and social play emerged, and any prenatal, birth, hearing, or medical issues, help distinguish typical variation from conditions such as language disorder, hearing loss, or autism spectrum disorder, and guide referrals.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Clinical interview: developmental and biopsychosocial history · Berk (Development Through the Lifespan) — Language and social development in early childhood
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

131. nce-s-ass-059 · Assessment and Testing · biopsychosocial history · medium · In review

During a biopsychosocial intake for her first episode of depression, a 22-year-old mentions that her mother was hospitalized for bipolar disorder. Why is this family history clinically important?
A. It confirms that the client has bipolar disorder herself
Family history raises risk but cannot establish a diagnosis; the client's own history must meet criteria.
B. It raises concern for bipolarity, so screening is key ✔ KEY
A first-degree relative with bipolar disorder increases risk, so past hypomania and future mood shifts need careful screening.
C. It is not relevant once the client is an adult living alone
Family psychiatric history keeps its relevance to risk regardless of the client's age or living situation.
D. It shows that the client's depression is mostly learned
Family history reflects genetic and environmental influences; it does not show that symptoms were learned.
Rationale: Family psychiatric history is a standard part of the biopsychosocial assessment. Bipolar disorder is strongly heritable, so a depressed client with a first-degree relative who has bipolar disorder warrants careful questioning about past hypomanic or manic symptoms and monitoring over time. The information also matters for any referral for medication evaluation, because antidepressants alone may carry risk in bipolar disorder.
References: DSM-5-TR — Bipolar I disorder: Risk and Prognostic Factors (genetic and physiological) · Hays (Assessment) — Clinical interview: family history
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

132. nce-s-ass-060 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · biopsychosocial history · medium · In review

Near the end of a biopsychosocial interview, a counselor asks a 58-year-old client about his friendships, his faith community, times he coped well in the past, and things he does well. What is the main purpose of gathering this information?
A. To estimate whether he qualifies for disability benefits
Benefit eligibility depends on functional limits and outside rules, not on a strengths inventory.
B. To screen him for grandiosity and inflated self-esteem
Asking about strengths is not a mania screen; grandiosity is assessed through mood history and the MSE.
C. To set the DSM-5-TR severity specifier for his diagnosis
Severity specifiers depend on symptom criteria, not on the client's supports or strengths.
D. To find resources that the treatment plan can build on ✔ KEY
Strengths, supports, and past coping successes are resources that inform goals and interventions.
Rationale: A complete biopsychosocial history covers not only problems and risks but also strengths, social supports, spiritual resources, and past coping. These protective factors shape a realistic, collaborative treatment plan, can support safety planning, and convey to the client that the counselor sees the whole person rather than a list of deficits.
References: Wiger (Documentation) — Biopsychosocial assessment: strengths and resources
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

133. nce-s-ass-061 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · intake interview structure · easy · In review

When structuring an initial intake interview, which sequence is generally recommended for exploring the client's concerns?
A. Begin with closed questions on the most sensitive topics
Starting with sensitive, closed questions before rapport tends to limit disclosure and raise anxiety.
B. Ask about trauma history before the presenting problem
The client's reason for coming usually comes first; detailed trauma questions follow once rapport is built.
C. Start with open questions, then narrow to specifics ✔ KEY
This funnel approach lets the client tell the story in their own words, then fills gaps with targeted questions.
D. Read a full symptom checklist before any open question
Leading with a checklist structures the interview around the form rather than the client's concerns.
Rationale: Most intake models use a funnel: after informed consent, the counselor invites the client to describe the presenting concern in their own words with open-ended questions, then narrows to specific questions about onset, duration, severity, and history. This builds rapport, captures the client's view of the problem, and still yields the detail needed for diagnosis and planning.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Clinical interviewing: structure and sequencing of the intake · Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — The initial interview
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

134. nce-s-ass-062 · Assessment and Testing · intake interview structure · medium · In review

An agency is deciding between a fully structured diagnostic interview and an unstructured clinical interview for its intakes. Which statement accurately compares the two approaches?
A. Structured interviews yield higher interrater reliability ✔ KEY
Fixed wording and order reduce variation between interviewers, which raises agreement on diagnoses.
B. Unstructured interviews are less open to clinician bias
Unstructured interviews depend more on clinician judgment, which makes them more open to bias.
C. Structured interviews let clinicians freely vary questions
Freedom to vary questions describes unstructured or semi-structured interviews, not fully structured ones.
D. Unstructured interviews are too unreliable to be of use
Unstructured interviews offer flexibility and rapport and remain widely used, despite lower reliability.
Rationale: Fully structured interviews ask set questions in a set order with set scoring, so different interviewers reach more similar conclusions (higher reliability). The tradeoff is less flexibility to follow the client's lead. Unstructured interviews offer flexibility and rapport but rely heavily on the clinician, which lowers reliability and leaves more room for bias. Semi-structured interviews fall between the two.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Clinical interviews: structured, semi-structured and unstructured formats
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

135. nce-s-ass-063 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · mental status examination · easy · In review

During a mental status examination, a client correctly gives her name and says she is in a hospital, but she cannot state the month, the year, or the day of the week. How should orientation be recorded?
A. Fully oriented in all three spheres
She cannot give the date, so she is not oriented to time.
B. Oriented to person and place, not time ✔ KEY
She knows who she is and where she is but not the date, so she is oriented to person and place only.
C. Oriented to time and place, not person
She correctly gave her own name, so orientation to person is intact.
D. Disoriented in all three spheres
She is oriented to both person and place, so she is not fully disoriented.
Rationale: Orientation in the MSE is usually checked for person, place, and time (sometimes also situation) and recorded as, for example, "oriented x2." Orientation to time is typically the first to be lost in delirium and dementia, while orientation to person is usually the last. Any disorientation warrants attention to possible medical or neurocognitive causes.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Mental status examination: sensorium and orientation
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

136. nce-s-ass-064 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · mental status examination · medium · In review

A 39-year-old client says, "I know my drinking is out of control, and it's hurting my kids." Later in the session she mentions that she drove her children to school that morning after drinking. How are insight and judgment BEST described in the mental status examination?
A. Insight is poor, but judgment is good
She recognizes the problem and its effects, so insight is not poor; driving after drinking is not good judgment.
B. Insight and judgment are both intact
Driving her children after drinking shows impaired judgment, despite her awareness.
C. Insight is absent, and judgment is poor
She names the problem and its harm to her children, so insight is present, not absent.
D. Insight fair, but judgment impaired ✔ KEY
She understands the problem (insight) but made a dangerous decision (judgment), so the two are rated differently.
Rationale: In the MSE, insight is the client's awareness that a problem exists and understanding of its causes and effects. Judgment is the ability to make sound decisions and anticipate consequences, best inferred from real recent behavior. The two can diverge: a client may describe a problem accurately yet still act in risky ways, as here.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Mental status examination: insight and judgment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

137. nce-s-ass-065 · Assessment and Testing · suicide and violence risk assessment · hard · In review

A 36-year-old client reports a plan to overdose this weekend on medication she has been saving and says she intends to act on it. She adds that her two children "are the reason I'm still here." How should the counselor weigh her children as a protective factor?
A. Note it, but treat risk as high and act on safety now ✔ KEY
Protective factors matter, but a plan with intent and means signals high acute risk that needs immediate action.
B. View it as reducing her risk to low; plan to meet next week
A single protective factor does not offset a specific plan, stated intent, and access to means.
C. Have her sign a no-harm contract, then end the session
No-suicide contracts are not supported as protection and do not address the plan or her access to means.
D. Set it aside, since protective factors do not change risk
Protective factors are part of a sound formulation and can be used in safety planning; they are not ignored.
Rationale: Suicide risk formulation weighs risk factors, warning signs, and protective factors together, but protective factors do not cancel out acute warning signs. Ideation with a specific plan, stated intent, and available means indicates high acute risk and calls for immediate safety steps, such as restricting means, involving supports, and arranging a higher level of care as needed. Her reasons for living can be built into the safety plan.
References: C-SSRS — Suicidal ideation with specific plan and intent · Stanley-Brown SPI — Reasons for living and means restriction
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

138. nce-s-ass-066 · Assessment and Testing · suicide and violence risk assessment · easy · In review

A counselor is assessing an adult client's risk of harming others. Which factor is generally considered the strongest single predictor of future violent behavior?
A. Having any diagnosed mental disorder
Most people with mental disorders are not violent; diagnosis alone is a weak predictor.
B. A score below average on an IQ test
Intelligence test scores are not a strong or direct predictor of violence.
C. A history of past violent behavior ✔ KEY
Past violence is the most consistently supported predictor of future violence.
D. Living alone, away from family members
Living alone is not an established predictor of violence toward others.
Rationale: In violence risk assessment, past behavior is the best predictor of future behavior: a history of violence, especially recent, frequent, or severe violence, carries the most weight. Other factors that raise risk include substance use, stated threats or intent, access to weapons, and certain active symptoms, such as command hallucinations or paranoid beliefs about a specific person.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Risk assessment: violence and harm to others
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

139. nce-s-ass-067 · Assessment and Testing · DSM-5-TR diagnostic structure and specifiers · medium · In review

A 20-year-old has had delusions, hallucinations, and disorganized speech for two months. The symptoms continue, and it is not yet known whether he will recover within six months. Which diagnosis is MOST appropriate now?
A. Schizophrenia, first episode
Schizophrenia requires continuous signs of disturbance for at least six months.
B. Brief psychotic disorder
Brief psychotic disorder lasts at least one day but less than one month.
C. Schizoaffective disorder
No major mood episode is described, which schizoaffective disorder requires.
D. Schizophreniform disorder (provisional) ✔ KEY
Symptoms of one to six months with recovery not yet known call for a provisional schizophreniform diagnosis.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR uses "provisional" when there is a strong presumption that full criteria will be met but not enough information is yet available. Schizophreniform disorder lasts at least one month but less than six. When the diagnosis must be made before recovery is known, it is labeled provisional; if symptoms reach six months, the diagnosis changes to schizophrenia.
References: DSM-5-TR — Schizophreniform disorder: Diagnostic Criteria B; provisional diagnosis (Use of the Manual)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

140. nce-s-ass-068 · Human Growth and Development · DSM-5-TR diagnostic structure and specifiers · hard · In review

A counselor on a school evaluation team is documenting autism spectrum disorder for a 7-year-old using DSM-5-TR. How are the severity levels for this diagnosis assigned?
A. As a single overall level based on the child's IQ score
Intellectual impairment is recorded with its own specifier; it does not set autism severity.
B. Separately for social communication and restricted behavior ✔ KEY
Each of the two core domains receives its own level, from requiring support to requiring very substantial support.
C. By the total count of criteria the child meets across domains
Autism severity reflects the support needed, not a criteria count as in substance use disorders.
D. By how early in life the symptoms were first noticed by parents
Age of recognition is part of the history, but it does not determine the severity level.
Rationale: For autism spectrum disorder, DSM-5-TR rates current severity separately for social communication and for restricted, repetitive behaviors, using Level 1 ("requiring support"), Level 2 ("requiring substantial support"), and Level 3 ("requiring very substantial support"). The levels can differ between domains and can change over time. Accompanying intellectual or language impairment is recorded with separate specifiers.
References: DSM-5-TR — Autism spectrum disorder: severity levels and specifiers
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

141. nce-s-ass-069 · Assessment and Testing · intelligence and achievement tests · easy · In review

A clinic wants a single individually administered intelligence test it can use with clients ranging from a 4-year-old to a 70-year-old. Which instrument covers this full age range?
A. Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-V
The WISC-V is normed for school-age children (about 6 to 16), not preschoolers or older adults.
B. Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale-IV
The WPPSI-IV covers young children (about 2½ to 7), not adults.
C. Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales (SB5) ✔ KEY
The SB5 is normed from age 2 through 85 and older, covering both clients.
D. Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-IV
The WAIS-IV starts at age 16, so it cannot be used with a 4-year-old.
Rationale: The Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales, Fifth Edition (SB5), spans roughly ages 2 to 85+ and measures five factors (fluid reasoning, knowledge, quantitative reasoning, visual-spatial processing, and working memory) in both verbal and nonverbal domains. The Wechsler scales instead use separate tests by age band: WPPSI for preschoolers, WISC for school-age children, and WAIS for older adolescents and adults.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Intelligence testing: Stanford-Binet Fifth Edition and the Wechsler scales
⚑ Check: Age ranges stated approximately (SB5 2-85+, WISC-V 6-16, WPPSI-IV 2:6-7:7, WAIS-IV 16-90); a WAIS-5 has since been published with a similar adult range. SME to confirm editions.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

142. nce-s-ass-070 · Assessment and Testing · intelligence and achievement tests · medium · In review

A 10-year-old's WISC-V Full Scale IQ is 112, while her reading standard score on the Woodcock-Johnson IV Tests of Achievement is 78. Both scales have a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. What has this pattern traditionally been taken to suggest?
A. A possible specific learning disability in reading ✔ KEY
A large gap between average-or-better ability and low achievement is the classic ability-achievement discrepancy.
B. Mild intellectual disability that affects reading
An IQ of 112 is above average, which rules out intellectual disability.
C. Invalid testing, as the two scores should match
Ability and achievement measure different things; a gap is meaningful, not proof of invalid testing.
D. Above-average reading skill for a child of her age
A standard score of 78 is about 1.5 SD below the mean, well below average.
Rationale: The ability-achievement discrepancy model compares an intelligence score (such as WISC-V FSIQ) with an achievement score (such as on the WIAT or Woodcock-Johnson). A gap of more than two standard deviations, as here (34 points), was long used to identify a specific learning disability. IDEA 2004 no longer requires schools to use a discrepancy and permits response-to-intervention approaches, and DSM-5-TR does not require a discrepancy.
References: Hays (Assessment) — Achievement testing: ability-achievement discrepancy and learning disabilities
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

143. nce-s-ass-071 · Social and Cultural Diversity · culturally fair assessment · medium · In review

A counselor wants to use an English-language anxiety inventory with Vietnamese-speaking clients and asks a bilingual staff member to translate it word for word. What is the MOST important limitation of this plan?
A. Any translated test loses its reliability completely
Translation does not erase reliability by definition; it must be re-examined in the new version.
B. Translation alone does not ensure equivalence or norms ✔ KEY
Items may change meaning across languages, and English-speaking norms may not apply to the new group.
C. Clients must take it in English to compare to the norms
Testing in a client's weaker language threatens validity; it is not the solution.
D. Anxiety cannot be assessed across different cultures
Anxiety can be assessed cross-culturally with suitably adapted and validated measures.
Rationale: Culturally fair assessment requires more than literal translation. Adapted tests need linguistic, conceptual, and metric equivalence, usually established through processes such as back-translation and review by bilingual experts, followed by evidence of reliability and validity with the new population. Scores should also be interpreted against appropriate norms; ACA Code E.8 calls for caution when using instruments normed on other populations.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — E.8 Multicultural Issues/Diversity in Assessment · Hays (Assessment) — Culturally fair assessment: test translation and equivalence
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

144. nce-s-ass-072 · Social and Cultural Diversity · culturally fair assessment · hard · In review

A 30-year-old client of Puerto Rican heritage describes an episode at her father's funeral in which she screamed uncontrollably, trembled, felt heat rising in her chest, and briefly felt detached, then felt like herself again. Which approach BEST reflects culturally fair assessment?
A. Diagnose panic disorder based on the physical symptoms she reports
One episode tied to a stressful event does not meet panic disorder criteria, and cultural meaning is not explored.
B. Record it as a dissociative disorder due to the brief detachment
Brief detachment within a culturally recognized distress episode does not establish a dissociative disorder.
C. Note it as a psychotic episode given the loss of control described
Nothing in the episode suggests delusions or hallucinations; loss of control is not psychosis.
D. Explore it as a possible cultural idiom of distress before labeling ✔ KEY
The pattern matches ataque de nervios, a cultural concept of distress, so its meaning should be explored first.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR describes ataque de nervios as a cultural concept of distress common among people of Latin American, and especially Caribbean, heritage. It often follows a stressful family event and can include uncontrollable shouting, crying, trembling, heat rising to the head or chest, and brief dissociation, with a quick return to usual functioning. Exploring the client's own explanation, for example with the Cultural Formulation Interview, guards against misdiagnosing culturally shaped distress.
References: DSM-5-TR — Culture and Psychiatric Diagnosis: cultural concepts of distress (ataque de nervios) · Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Culturally appropriate assessment and diagnosis
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

Areas of Clinical Focus

177 items · NCE weight 29% (47 of 160 scored items)

145. nce-s-clf-001 · Assessment and Testing · depressive disorders · easy · In review

Under DSM-5-TR, what is the minimum duration for the symptoms of a major depressive episode?
A. One week
One week is the minimum duration for a manic episode, not a major depressive episode.
B. Two weeks ✔ KEY
A major depressive episode requires five or more symptoms present during the same 2-week period.
C. One month
One month is not the major depressive episode threshold; it is used for other diagnoses, such as the active phase of schizophrenia.
D. Six months
Six months is the duration for generalized anxiety disorder, not a major depressive episode.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR requires at least five of nine symptoms, including depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure, present nearly every day during the same 2-week period and representing a change from prior functioning. Knowing duration thresholds helps counselors tell a depressive episode apart from shorter, situational low mood.
References: DSM-5-TR — Major Depressive Disorder, Criterion A
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

146. nce-s-clf-002 · Assessment and Testing · depressive disorders · medium · In review

A 41-year-old client reports feeling down more days than not for the past 3 years, with low energy, poor appetite, and hopelessness. She cannot recall a stretch of more than a few weeks without these symptoms and has never had a manic or hypomanic episode. Full criteria for a major depressive episode have not been met. Which diagnosis BEST fits?
A. Cyclothymic disorder
Cyclothymic disorder requires numerous periods of hypomanic symptoms alongside depressive symptoms; she reports no elevated mood.
B. Adjustment disorder with depressed mood
Adjustment disorder follows an identifiable stressor and does not persist more than 6 months after the stressor ends; this is a chronic 3-year pattern.
C. Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder
DMDD is a childhood diagnosis (first given between ages 6 and 18, onset before 10) marked by severe temper outbursts.
D. Persistent depressive disorder ✔ KEY
Depressed mood more days than not for at least 2 years in an adult, with two or more associated symptoms and no symptom-free period longer than 2 months, fits persistent depressive disorder.
Rationale: Persistent depressive disorder requires depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years in adults (1 year in children and adolescents), plus at least two associated symptoms such as appetite change, low energy, or hopelessness. During that period the person has not been without symptoms for more than 2 months at a time, and there has never been a manic or hypomanic episode.
References: DSM-5-TR — Persistent Depressive Disorder, Criteria A–C
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

147. nce-s-clf-003 · Human Growth and Development · depressive disorders · hard · In review

A 15-year-old has shown irritable mood on most days for the past 14 months, along with low self-esteem and poor concentration. He has not gone more than a few weeks without these symptoms, has no history of severe temper outbursts, and has never met criteria for a manic or hypomanic episode. Which statement is MOST accurate?
A. Criteria for persistent depressive disorder can be met at this point ✔ KEY
For children and adolescents, mood may be irritable and the duration requirement is 1 year, so 14 months is sufficient.
B. Persistent depressive disorder requires 2 full years in any age group
The 2-year requirement applies to adults; DSM-5-TR shortens it to 1 year for children and adolescents.
C. Irritable rather than sad mood rules out a depressive disorder diagnosis
DSM-5-TR allows irritable mood to satisfy the mood criterion for depressive disorders in children and adolescents.
D. Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder is the required diagnosis here
DMDD requires severe, recurrent temper outbursts with onset before age 10, which this teen does not show.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR modifies persistent depressive disorder for youth in two ways: mood can be irritable rather than depressed, and the minimum duration is 1 year instead of 2. Counselors working with adolescents should recognize that chronic irritability can be a depressive presentation rather than simply a behavior problem.
References: DSM-5-TR — Persistent Depressive Disorder, Criterion A (children and adolescents)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

148. nce-s-clf-004 · Assessment and Testing · bipolar disorders · easy · In review

Unless hospitalization is required, what is the minimum duration of a manic episode in DSM-5-TR?
A. Four consecutive days
Four consecutive days is the minimum for a hypomanic episode, not a manic episode.
B. Two weeks
Two weeks is the duration requirement for a major depressive episode.
C. One week ✔ KEY
A manic episode lasts at least 1 week and is present most of the day, nearly every day, or any duration if hospitalization is needed.
D. One month
One month is not a mood episode threshold; it is too long for mania.
Rationale: A manic episode is a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood plus increased activity or energy lasting at least 1 week (any duration if hospitalization is necessary). A hypomanic episode needs only 4 consecutive days and does not cause marked impairment or require hospitalization.
References: DSM-5-TR — Bipolar I Disorder, Manic Episode Criterion A
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

149. nce-s-clf-005 · Assessment and Testing · bipolar disorders · medium · In review

A 30-year-old client has had two major depressive episodes. Last spring she had 5 days of unusually elevated mood, less need for sleep, and increased productivity that friends noticed but that did not impair her work or require hospitalization. She has never had psychotic symptoms or a longer elevated period. Which diagnosis is MOST appropriate?
A. Bipolar II disorder ✔ KEY
At least one hypomanic episode (4+ days, no marked impairment) plus at least one major depressive episode, with no history of mania, defines bipolar II disorder.
B. Bipolar I disorder
Bipolar I requires at least one full manic episode; her elevated period was hypomanic.
C. Cyclothymic disorder
Cyclothymic disorder requires symptoms that never meet full criteria for a major depressive episode; she has had two.
D. Major depressive disorder
A history of a hypomanic episode excludes a diagnosis of major depressive disorder.
Rationale: Bipolar II disorder requires at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, with no lifetime manic episode. Hypomania lasts at least 4 consecutive days, is observable by others, and is not severe enough to cause marked impairment or hospitalization. Screening for past hypomania is essential before treating depression as unipolar.
References: DSM-5-TR — Bipolar II Disorder, Criteria A–B; Hypomanic Episode
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

150. nce-s-clf-006 · Assessment and Testing · bipolar disorders · hard · In review

A 27-year-old with no prior psychiatric history develops grandiosity, pressured speech, almost no sleep, and reckless spending. On the third day he is psychiatrically hospitalized because his behavior has become dangerous. Substances and medical causes are ruled out. Which statement is MOST accurate?
A. The episode is hypomanic because it lasted fewer than 4 days
Hypomania itself requires at least 4 days and, by definition, does not require hospitalization.
B. No bipolar diagnosis applies until symptoms reach 1 full week
The 1-week requirement is waived when hospitalization is necessary.
C. Bipolar I also requires a prior major depressive episode on record
A single manic episode is sufficient for bipolar I; a depressive episode is common but not required.
D. The episode is manic since hospitalization waives the duration ✔ KEY
DSM-5-TR counts a manic episode of any duration if hospitalization is necessary, so bipolar I disorder can be diagnosed.
Rationale: The 1-week duration for a manic episode applies unless hospitalization is necessary, in which case any duration qualifies. Bipolar I disorder requires only one lifetime manic episode; major depressive episodes are common but are not required for the diagnosis.
References: DSM-5-TR — Bipolar I Disorder, Manic Episode Criterion A and Criterion for Bipolar I
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

151. nce-s-clf-007 · Assessment and Testing · anxiety disorders · easy · In review

For a diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder, excessive anxiety and worry must occur more days than not for at least how long?
A. 1 month
One month is the post-attack worry period for panic disorder, not the GAD duration.
B. 6 months ✔ KEY
GAD requires excessive anxiety and worry more days than not for at least 6 months.
C. 3 months
Three months is not the GAD threshold.
D. 2 years
Two years is the adult duration for persistent depressive disorder.
Rationale: Generalized anxiety disorder involves excessive, hard-to-control worry about a number of events or activities, occurring more days than not for at least 6 months, with three or more associated symptoms in adults (only one in children), such as restlessness, fatigue, or sleep disturbance.
References: DSM-5-TR — Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Criterion A
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

152. nce-s-clf-008 · Assessment and Testing · anxiety disorders · medium · In review

A 36-year-old client has had several sudden, unexpected surges of intense fear with a pounding heart, shortness of breath, and dizziness. For the past 2 months he has worried constantly about having another attack and has stopped exercising because a racing heart might trigger one. Medical causes have been ruled out. Which diagnosis BEST fits?
A. Panic disorder ✔ KEY
Recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by at least 1 month of persistent worry or maladaptive behavior change define panic disorder.
B. Agoraphobia
Agoraphobia requires fear or avoidance in at least two situations such as crowds or public transit; his avoidance centers on bodily sensations.
C. Illness anxiety disorder
Illness anxiety centers on a preoccupation with having a serious illness, not on recurrent unexpected panic attacks.
D. Specific phobia, situational
Specific phobia involves fear cued by a particular object or situation, whereas these attacks are unexpected.
Rationale: Panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected panic attacks, with at least one attack followed by 1 month or more of persistent concern about further attacks or their consequences, or a significant maladaptive change in behavior such as avoiding exercise. Interoceptive avoidance like this is a common target of cognitive behavioral treatment.
References: DSM-5-TR — Panic Disorder, Criteria A–B · Barlow PCT — Interoceptive avoidance and exposure
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

153. nce-s-clf-009 · Assessment and Testing · trauma- and stressor-related disorders · medium · In review

Ten days after a serious highway collision, a 24-year-old reports intrusive memories, nightmares, feeling as if the world is unreal, avoiding driving, and trouble sleeping and concentrating. The symptoms began right after the crash and are impairing her work. Which diagnosis is MOST appropriate at this time?
A. Posttraumatic stress disorder
PTSD requires symptoms lasting more than 1 month; only 10 days have passed.
B. Adjustment disorder with anxiety
When symptoms meet criteria for a trauma-specific disorder, adjustment disorder is not the best fit.
C. Acute stress disorder ✔ KEY
Acute stress disorder applies when trauma-related symptoms last from 3 days to 1 month after exposure.
D. Generalized anxiety disorder
GAD involves diffuse worry for at least 6 months and is not tied to a traumatic event.
Rationale: Acute stress disorder is diagnosed when nine or more symptoms across intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and arousal last from 3 days to 1 month after trauma exposure. If symptoms persist beyond 1 month and meet PTSD criteria, the diagnosis is changed to PTSD.
References: DSM-5-TR — Acute Stress Disorder, Criteria B–C
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

154. nce-s-clf-010 · Assessment and Testing · trauma- and stressor-related disorders · hard · In review

A firefighter developed some sleep problems and irritability soon after a fatal fire. Eight months later, after more symptoms emerged, she meets full criteria for PTSD for the first time. She does not report depersonalization or derealization. Which specifier applies?
A. With dissociative symptoms
The dissociative specifier requires persistent depersonalization or derealization, which she denies.
B. With panic attacks
The with-panic-attacks specifier requires panic attacks alongside the disorder, and none are described here.
C. With acute onset
DSM-5-TR PTSD has no acute-onset specifier; the DSM-IV acute and chronic specifiers were removed.
D. With delayed expression ✔ KEY
This specifier is used when full criteria are not met until at least 6 months after the event, even if some symptoms began earlier.
Rationale: In DSM-5-TR, PTSD "with delayed expression" is specified when full diagnostic criteria are not met until at least 6 months after the event, although the onset and expression of some symptoms may be immediate. The other PTSD specifier is "with dissociative symptoms" (depersonalization or derealization).
References: DSM-5-TR — Posttraumatic Stress Disorder, specifiers
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

155. nce-s-clf-011 · Assessment and Testing · obsessive-compulsive and related disorders · medium · In review

A client with contamination obsessions washes his hands for hours daily. He says his family will probably become seriously ill if he stops washing, although he admits he could be wrong. Which DSM-5-TR insight specifier is MOST accurate?
A. With good or fair insight
Good or fair insight means the person recognizes the beliefs are definitely or probably not true.
B. With poor insight ✔ KEY
Poor insight applies when the person thinks the OCD beliefs are probably true.
C. With absent insight
Absent insight/delusional beliefs applies when the person is completely convinced the beliefs are true; he admits doubt.
D. With tic-related features
The tic-related specifier concerns a current or past tic disorder, not the degree of insight.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR rates insight in OCD on three levels: good or fair (beliefs definitely or probably not true), poor (beliefs probably true), and absent insight/delusional beliefs (completely convinced the beliefs are true). A separate "tic-related" specifier notes a current or past tic disorder.
References: DSM-5-TR — Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, insight specifiers
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

156. nce-s-clf-012 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · obsessive-compulsive and related disorders · easy · In review

Which psychological intervention has the strongest evidence as a first-line treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder?
A. Insight-oriented psychodynamic therapy
Psychodynamic therapy lacks the evidence base that exposure-based CBT has for OCD.
B. Thought stopping with reassurance
Reassurance acts as a compulsion and maintains OCD; thought stopping tends to backfire.
C. Exposure and response prevention ✔ KEY
ERP, a form of CBT, exposes clients to feared cues while they refrain from compulsions and is the first-line psychological treatment.
D. Nondirective supportive counseling
Supportive counseling alone does not target the obsession–compulsion cycle.
Rationale: Exposure and response prevention has clients face feared thoughts, images, or situations while resisting compulsions, allowing anxiety to decline without the ritual and weakening the negative reinforcement that maintains OCD. Reassurance-giving by the counselor or family is itself a compulsion to be reduced.
References: NICE guidelines — CG31 Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: CBT including ERP
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

157. nce-s-clf-013 · Assessment and Testing · substance use and addictive disorders · medium · In review

Over the past 12 months, a client has met five of the eleven DSM-5-TR criteria for alcohol use disorder. Which severity specifier applies?
A. Mild
Mild applies when two or three criteria are met.
B. Severe
Severe applies when six or more criteria are met.
C. Moderate ✔ KEY
Moderate applies when four or five criteria are met.
D. Subthreshold
Two criteria within 12 months are enough for a diagnosis, so five is well above threshold.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR substance use disorders require at least two of eleven criteria within a 12-month period. Severity is specified as mild (2–3 criteria), moderate (4–5), or severe (6 or more). Severity guides level-of-care decisions alongside a dimensional assessment such as the ASAM Criteria.
References: DSM-5-TR — Alcohol Use Disorder, severity specifiers
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

158. nce-s-clf-014 · Assessment and Testing · substance use and addictive disorders · medium · In review

A 52-year-old takes a prescribed opioid exactly as directed for chronic back pain under a physician's care. She reports needing a higher dose than at first and feeling withdrawal symptoms if a dose is late. No other use disorder criteria are present. How should the counselor understand these symptoms?
A. They are not counted toward an opioid use disorder ✔ KEY
Tolerance and withdrawal are not counted when the opioid is taken solely under appropriate medical supervision.
B. They meet criteria for mild opioid use disorder
Two counted criteria would be mild, but these two are excluded in supervised medical use.
C. They confirm a severe opioid use disorder is present
Physiological dependence alone does not establish any use disorder, let alone a severe one.
D. They point to opioid use disorder in remission
Remission requires a prior full use disorder, which has not been established.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR notes that tolerance and withdrawal are expected physiological adaptations when medications such as opioids, sedatives, or stimulants are taken as prescribed under medical supervision, and they are not counted toward a use disorder in that situation. A diagnosis requires other evidence of problematic use, such as craving or loss of control.
References: DSM-5-TR — Opioid Use Disorder, Criteria 10–11 note on medical supervision
⚑ Check: The cited 'Criteria 10-11 note' detail is the writer's wording of where the DSM-5-TR note sits.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

159. nce-s-clf-015 · Human Growth and Development · neurodevelopmental disorders · easy · In review

Under DSM-5-TR, several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms of ADHD must have been present before what age?
A. Age 7
Onset before age 7 was the DSM-IV standard; DSM-5 raised it to 12.
B. Age 12 ✔ KEY
DSM-5-TR requires several symptoms to have been present before age 12.
C. Age 16
Age 16 is not a criterion; age 17 marks where the adult symptom count of five applies.
D. Age 18
Age 18 is not the ADHD onset threshold.
Rationale: ADHD requires several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms before age 12, present in two or more settings, with clear interference in functioning. Children need six symptoms in a domain; adolescents 17 and older and adults need five. Adult assessment therefore includes a developmental history.
References: DSM-5-TR — Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Criteria A and C
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

160. nce-s-clf-016 · Human Growth and Development · neurodevelopmental disorders · hard · In review

A 7-year-old struggles to take turns in conversation, misses jokes and hints, and speaks to teachers the same way he speaks to peers. A counselor is weighing autism spectrum disorder against social (pragmatic) communication disorder. Which finding would MOST support autism spectrum disorder?
A. Late onset of first spoken words
Language delay can occur in many conditions and is not a defining criterion that separates the two.
B. Trouble using language socially
Difficulty with social use of language is central to both disorders, so it does not distinguish them.
C. Below-average intellectual ability
Intellectual impairment is a possible specifier for ASD but is neither required nor distinguishing.
D. Restricted, repetitive behaviors ✔ KEY
ASD requires restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities; their presence rules out SCD.
Rationale: Both ASD and social (pragmatic) communication disorder involve deficits in social communication. ASD also requires at least two kinds of restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities (such as rigid routines, intense interests, or sensory differences). SCD is diagnosed only when such patterns are absent, past or present.
References: DSM-5-TR — Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder, Criterion D; Autism Spectrum Disorder, Criterion B
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

161. nce-s-clf-017 · Assessment and Testing · schizophrenia spectrum disorders · medium · In review

A 22-year-old college student has had auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions, and disorganized speech for about 3 months, including any early warning signs. There have been no mood episodes, and substance and medical causes are ruled out. Which diagnosis is MOST appropriate?
A. Schizophreniform disorder ✔ KEY
Schizophreniform disorder has schizophrenia-like symptoms lasting at least 1 month but less than 6 months.
B. Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia requires continuous signs of disturbance for at least 6 months.
C. Brief psychotic disorder
Brief psychotic disorder lasts at least 1 day but less than 1 month, with full return to functioning.
D. Delusional disorder
Delusional disorder involves delusions without prominent hallucinations or disorganized speech.
Rationale: The schizophrenia spectrum is partly sorted by duration: brief psychotic disorder lasts 1 day to less than 1 month; schizophreniform disorder lasts 1 month to less than 6 months; schizophrenia requires at least 6 months of disturbance, including at least 1 month of active-phase symptoms.
References: DSM-5-TR — Schizophreniform Disorder, Criteria A–B
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

162. nce-s-clf-018 · Assessment and Testing · schizophrenia spectrum disorders · hard · In review

A 26-year-old has had 5 weeks of prominent hallucinations and delusions. His family reports that for about 6 months before that, he withdrew from friends, showed flat affect, and voiced odd beliefs. No mood episodes have occurred, and substance and medical causes are excluded. Which diagnosis BEST fits?
A. Schizophreniform disorder
The prodromal period counts toward duration, so the total exceeds the less-than-6-months limit for schizophreniform disorder.
B. Schizophrenia ✔ KEY
More than 1 month of active symptoms plus a prodromal period gives over 6 months of continuous disturbance.
C. Brief psychotic disorder
Brief psychotic disorder lasts less than 1 month in total; the active phase alone is longer.
D. Schizoaffective disorder
Schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with psychotic symptoms; none occurred.
Rationale: Schizophrenia requires continuous signs of disturbance for at least 6 months, which must include at least 1 month of active-phase symptoms and may include prodromal or residual periods with negative symptoms or attenuated positive symptoms. Collateral history from family is often essential for establishing the prodromal phase.
References: DSM-5-TR — Schizophrenia, Criterion C
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

163. nce-s-clf-019 · Assessment and Testing · personality disorders · easy · In review

Which personality disorder belongs to DSM-5-TR Cluster C (the anxious or fearful cluster)?
A. Schizotypal personality disorder
Schizotypal is in Cluster A, the odd or eccentric cluster.
B. Histrionic personality disorder
Histrionic is in Cluster B, the dramatic, emotional, or erratic cluster.
C. Avoidant personality disorder ✔ KEY
Avoidant personality disorder is in Cluster C with dependent and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders.
D. Paranoid personality disorder
Paranoid is in Cluster A with schizoid and schizotypal.
Rationale: DSM-5-TR groups personality disorders into three clusters: A (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal) for odd or eccentric patterns; B (antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic) for dramatic or erratic patterns; and C (avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive) for anxious or fearful patterns.
References: DSM-5-TR — Personality Disorders, cluster groupings
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

164. nce-s-clf-020 · Assessment and Testing · personality disorders · medium · In review

A 20-year-old shows a pervasive pattern of deceitfulness, impulsivity, repeated fights, and lack of remorse since age 15. To diagnose antisocial personality disorder, which additional finding does DSM-5-TR require?
A. A documented history of arrest or jail
Legal involvement is common but not required; failure to conform to social norms can be shown in other ways.
B. No co-occurring substance use disorder
Substance use disorders frequently co-occur and do not rule out antisocial personality disorder.
C. Onset of the pattern after age 18 only
The pattern must be evident since age 15; onset is not restricted to adulthood.
D. Evidence of conduct disorder before 15 ✔ KEY
DSM-5-TR requires evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15, and the person must be at least 18.
Rationale: Antisocial personality disorder requires a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others occurring since age 15, a current age of at least 18, and evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15. The behavior must not occur only during schizophrenia or bipolar disorder.
References: DSM-5-TR — Antisocial Personality Disorder, Criteria B–C
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

165. nce-s-clf-021 · Assessment and Testing · eating disorders · medium · In review

A 33-year-old describes episodes, about twice a week for 6 months, of eating far more than most people would in a short period while feeling unable to stop. She eats rapidly, eats alone out of embarrassment, and feels disgusted afterward. She does not vomit, fast, misuse laxatives, or exercise to compensate. Which diagnosis BEST fits?
A. Bulimia nervosa
Bulimia nervosa requires recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors, which she does not use.
B. Binge-eating disorder ✔ KEY
Recurrent binges with loss of control and marked distress, at least weekly for 3 months, without regular compensatory behavior, fit binge-eating disorder.
C. ARFID
ARFID involves restricted intake, not binge episodes.
D. Anorexia nervosa, binge/purge type
Anorexia nervosa requires restriction leading to significantly low body weight and fear of weight gain, none of which is described, and she does not purge.
Rationale: Binge-eating disorder requires recurrent binge episodes with a sense of loss of control, three or more associated features (such as eating rapidly, eating alone from embarrassment, or feeling disgusted afterward), marked distress, and a frequency of at least once a week for 3 months. Unlike bulimia nervosa, there are no recurrent compensatory behaviors.
References: DSM-5-TR — Binge-Eating Disorder, Criteria A–E
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

166. nce-s-clf-022 · Human Growth and Development · eating disorders · medium · In review
