In Kanel's ABC model of crisis intervention, a counselor first builds rapport through attending and reflection. The counselor then identifies the precipitating event, the client's perception of it and the resulting distress and impaired functioning. What is this second phase called?
A. Boiling down the problem ✔ KEY
The B phase narrows the focus to the trigger, the client's perception and the subjective distress.
B. Coping
Coping is the C phase, which follows and focuses on current and new coping strategies.
C. Achieving contact
Achieving contact is the A phase, the rapport building described first in the stem.
D. Brief safety planning
Safety is assessed throughout but is not the name of a phase in the ABC model.
Rationale: Kanel's ABC model has three phases: A, achieving (developing and maintaining) contact; B, boiling down the problem by identifying the precipitating event, perceptions and distress; and C, coping, in which the counselor explores past and new coping and builds a plan. Its focus on perception reflects the view that crises arise from how events are interpreted.
References: Kanel (A Guide to Crisis Intervention) — ABC model: A, achieving contact; B, boiling down the problem; C, coping
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

540. nce-s-cou-168 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group stages and dynamics · medium · In review

Before launching a support group at a refugee resettlement agency, a counselor studies the community's needs, the agency's resources and support, and cultural attitudes toward discussing personal problems in a group. In the ASGW Best Practice Guidelines, this planning task is called:
A. Pre-group screening
Screening assesses individual prospective members, not the community and organizational context.
B. Ecological assessment ✔ KEY
ASGW asks group workers to assess the community, agency and cultural context before forming a group.
C. Professional disclosure
Professional disclosure informs members about the leader and the group; it is not a needs assessment.
D. Group processing
Processing is the later, ongoing reflection on what happens in sessions.
Rationale: The ASGW Best Practice Guidelines organize group work into planning, performing and group processing. In planning, an ecological assessment of community needs, organizational support and cultural factors guides whether and how a group is offered. Processing, by contrast, means regular reflection on sessions with co-leaders, members or supervisors.
References: ASGW Best Practice Guidelines — Best Practice in Planning: ecological assessment
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

541. nce-s-cou-169 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group stages and dynamics · easy · In review

The T-group (training group), first developed at the National Training Laboratories in Bethel, Maine, used here-and-now feedback to teach human relations skills. Whose field theory and group dynamics research led to this movement?
A. Carl Rogers
Rogers developed the basic encounter group, which grew alongside but separately from T-groups.
B. Jacob Moreno
Moreno developed psychodrama and is credited with coining the term group therapy.
C. Joseph Pratt
Pratt led early educational "classes" for patients with tuberculosis in the early 1900s.
D. Kurt Lewin ✔ KEY
Lewin's field theory and group dynamics work led his colleagues to found NTL and the T-group.
Rationale: Kurt Lewin studied how group forces shape individual behavior. His work led to the National Training Laboratories in 1947, where T-groups used here-and-now feedback to build interpersonal awareness. Rogers later extended the experiential group into the encounter group movement.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — History of group work: Lewin, T-groups and encounter groups
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

542. nce-s-cou-170 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group stages and dynamics · easy · In review

A counselor suggests that a recently widowed client try a community bereavement group run by and for people who have lost a spouse, with no professional leader. Compared with a counseling or therapy group, what BEST characterizes this kind of group?
A. It uses a professional leader trained to treat diagnosable mental disorders
This describes a psychotherapy group, not a peer-run group.
B. It follows a strict time-limited format with formal screening of all members
Mutual-aid groups are usually open and ongoing, without formal clinical screening.
C. It is peer-led, with members who share a concern offering one another support ✔ KEY
Self-help and mutual-aid groups are led by members who share the problem and help one another.
D. It focuses mainly on reshaping personality through deep insight and analysis
Reconstructive personality change is a goal of some long-term therapy groups, not of mutual-aid groups.
Rationale: Self-help and mutual-aid groups, such as Alcoholics Anonymous or widow-to-widow programs, are organized around a shared concern and led by members rather than professionals. They emphasize support, hope, universality and practical help, and they can complement rather than replace professional counseling.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Group work: self-help and mutual-aid groups
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

543. nce-s-cou-171 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group leadership skills and therapeutic factors · medium · In review

A 15-year-old in a court-mandated anger management group sits with his hood up and says, 'I'm only here because the judge made me.' What is the leader's BEST initial response?
A. Acknowledge he did not choose to come and invite him to say how that feels ✔ KEY
Openly naming involuntary status respects his autonomy and turns resistance into material for the group.
B. Explain that members who do not take part may be reported back to the court
Leading with threats reinforces the power struggle and deepens resistance.
C. Ask the other members to persuade him that the group will really help him
Recruiting peers to convince him puts him on the spot and can feel like ganging up.
D. Ignore the remark and move on so he gets no attention for his resistance
Ignoring a direct statement misses a chance to engage him and may model avoidance.
Rationale: Adolescents, and especially involuntary members, often test leaders and guard their autonomy. Acknowledging their reluctance openly, respecting choices about what to disclose and inviting them to talk about being sent helps build trust and often reduces resistance more than pressure or avoidance.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Group work with adolescents and involuntary members
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

544. nce-s-cou-172 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group stages and dynamics · medium · In review

In the ninth session of a cohesive interpersonal group, Malik tells Rosa that her advice-giving feels 'preachy,' and Rosa responds sharply. The room goes quiet. What should the leader do?
A. Move on to a new topic to protect the cohesion the group has built so far
Avoiding conflict teaches members that strong feelings are unsafe and wastes useful material.
B. Help both speak directly to each other and explore what the exchange stirs up ✔ KEY
Keeping the conflict in the here-and-now with direct communication makes it a source of learning.
C. Ask Malik and Rosa to work out their disagreement privately after the session
Moving conflict outside the group fosters subgrouping and removes it from shared work.
D. Point out that Malik's feedback was too harsh and ask him to rephrase it now
Taking sides shuts down exploration and positions the leader as judge.
Rationale: Yalom notes that conflict is inevitable and, in a cohesive group, can be highly productive. The leader keeps it in the here-and-now, encourages members to speak directly and own their reactions, and helps the group examine what the exchange reveals about each person's interpersonal patterns.
References: Yalom & Leszcz (Group Psychotherapy) — Conflict in the therapy group (the advanced group)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

545. nce-s-cou-173 · Group Counseling and Group Work · group leadership skills and therapeutic factors · medium · In review

A member describes feeling ignored at family dinners. The leader asks her, 'Is there anyone in this room who you feel might be ignoring you right now?' In Yalom's two-tiered approach to the here-and-now, this question is an example of:
A. Process illumination
Illumination is the second tier, in which the group reflects on and makes sense of what has happened.
B. Universality
Universality is a therapeutic factor, the relief of learning others share one's problems.
C. Catharsis
Catharsis is the expression of strong emotion, not a leader technique for shifting focus.
D. Here-and-now activation ✔ KEY
Steering an outside concern into members' relationships in the room is the first, activating tier.
Rationale: Yalom describes two tiers of here-and-now work. The leader first activates the here-and-now by moving the focus from outside, past events to members' reactions to one another in the room. The leader then illuminates the process, helping members reflect on and understand what just occurred; activation without illumination yields emotion without learning.
References: Yalom & Leszcz (Group Psychotherapy) — Ch. 6: The here-and-now, activation and illumination of process
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

546. nce-s-cou-174 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · family systems theories (Bowen, structural, strategic) · medium · In review

A 9-year-old's frequent stomachaches keep his worried mother home from work. A therapist directs the boy to pretend to have a stomachache at set times and the mother to pretend to comfort him, turning the symptom into play while the mother takes back her caretaking role. This technique is MOST closely associated with:
A. Salvador Minuchin
Minuchin's structural therapy uses enactments, joining and boundary making rather than pretend directives.
B. Murray Bowen
Bowen emphasized differentiation, triangles and genograms, with the therapist as a calm coach.
C. Cloé Madanes ✔ KEY
Madanes developed pretend techniques within strategic family therapy.
D. Virginia Satir
Satir's experiential approach focuses on communication stances, self-esteem and sculpting.
Rationale: Madanes viewed some children's symptoms as attempts to help a parent that also upset the family hierarchy. Pretend techniques ask the child to pretend to have the symptom and the parent to pretend to help, making the symptom voluntary and playful so it loses its function and the parent resumes an appropriate caregiving role.
References: Goldenberg (Family Therapy) — Strategic family therapy: Madanes and pretend techniques
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

547. nce-s-cou-175 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · family systems theories (Bowen, structural, strategic) · medium · In review

In a group setting, a guide uses a client's family chronology to have members role-play scenes from the lives of the client's parents and grandparents, helping the client see them as people and let go of old learnings. This experiential technique, developed by Virginia Satir, is called:
A. Family reconstruction ✔ KEY
Satir's family reconstruction re-enacts multigenerational scenes to free the "star" from outdated patterns.
B. Psychodrama
Psychodrama, created by Jacob Moreno, uses role-play but is not Satir's multigenerational technique.
C. Family sculpting
Sculpting arranges members in a physical tableau of present relationships rather than re-enacting family history.
D. Genogram construction
A genogram maps multigenerational patterns on paper (associated with Bowen) and does not involve role-play.
Rationale: Satir's family reconstruction guides a "star" through key events in three generations, using a family chronology and role players. Family sculpting, also used by Satir and by Duhl and Kantor, positions members physically to show closeness, distance and power. Both are experiential techniques that make family patterns visible and felt.
References: Goldenberg (Family Therapy) — Experiential family therapy: Satir, family reconstruction and sculpting
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

548. nce-s-cou-176 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · family systems theories (Bowen, structural, strategic) · hard · In review

Parents of a 14-year-old have grounded him for longer and longer periods for breaking curfew, with no effect. In MRI brief therapy terms, which outcome would represent second-order change?
A. The parents extend the grounding from one week to a full month
More of the same solution is first-order change in degree, not in kind.
B. The family changes the rules governing how curfew is set and handled ✔ KEY
Altering the rules of the system itself is second-order change.
C. The parents add the loss of his phone to the grounding as a penalty
Adding another penalty stays within the same punitive pattern, so it is first-order.
D. The parents keep the same rules but enforce them more strictly
Stricter enforcement of unchanged rules is a first-order adjustment.
Rationale: Watzlawick, Weakland and Fisch distinguished first-order change, a change within a system whose rules stay the same, from second-order change, a change in the system's rules or structure. MRI therapists look for interventions such as reframing that interrupt "more of the same" attempted solutions.
References: Goldenberg (Family Therapy) — MRI interactional view: first-order and second-order change
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

549. nce-s-cou-177 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · behavior therapy · medium · In review

Parents decide to stop going into their 3-year-old's room when she cries at bedtime. On the second and third nights, her crying becomes louder and lasts longer than before. How should the counselor explain this?
A. Spontaneous recovery; the plan has failed and should be stopped now
Spontaneous recovery is the return of a behavior after extinction appeared complete; the plan has not failed.
B. Negative reinforcement; her crying is being made stronger by them
Nothing aversive is being removed after crying, so this is not negative reinforcement.
C. Punishment; ignoring the crying is causing her new emotional harm
Withholding attention is extinction, not punishment, and the increase is predictable.
D. Extinction burst; it is expected and fades if parents stay consistent ✔ KEY
A temporary surge in a behavior when reinforcement stops is an extinction burst.
Rationale: When a previously reinforced behavior no longer produces its reinforcer, it often increases in frequency or intensity before declining, a pattern called an extinction burst. If caregivers give in during the burst, they reinforce a more intense version of the behavior on an intermittent schedule, so consistency is essential.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Behavior therapy: operant extinction and the extinction burst
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

550. nce-s-cou-178 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · behavior therapy · hard · In review

To reduce a child's hand-biting, a behavior analyst delivers a token at the end of every 10-minute interval in which no hand-biting occurs, regardless of what else the child is doing. Which procedure is this?
A. DRA (alternative behavior)
DRA reinforces a specific replacement behavior, such as asking for help, rather than mere absence of the target.
B. DRL (low rates of behavior)
DRL reinforces the target behavior when it occurs at or below a set rate, for behaviors to reduce but not eliminate.
C. DRO (other behavior) ✔ KEY
DRO reinforces the absence of the target behavior over an interval.
D. Premack principle
The Premack principle uses a high-probability activity to reinforce a low-probability one.
Rationale: Differential reinforcement of other behavior (DRO) delivers reinforcement when the target behavior has not occurred for a set interval, sometimes called differential reinforcement of zero rates. DRA reinforces a specified alternative behavior, DRI an incompatible one and DRL a low rate of the target itself.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Behavior therapy: differential reinforcement procedures
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

551. nce-s-cou-179 · Human Growth and Development · psychodynamic and psychoanalytic theory · medium · In review

An 18-month-old who recently toddled off happily to explore now repeatedly returns to his mother, shadows her, wants her to share each discovery and becomes upset when she leaves, yet sometimes pushes her away. In Mahler's separation-individuation theory, he is in which subphase?
A. Rapprochement ✔ KEY
Around 16 to 24 months, awareness of separateness brings renewed clinging alongside a push for autonomy.
B. Practicing
Practicing (about 10 to 16 months) is the earlier, exhilarated period of exploring with little concern for the mother.
C. Differentiation
Differentiation (about 5 to 10 months) is when the infant first begins to distinguish self from mother.
D. Object constancy
Object constancy (about 24 to 36 months) brings a stable inner image of the mother that eases separations.
Rationale: Mahler described separation-individuation subphases following the early autistic and symbiotic phases: differentiation, practicing, rapprochement and the move toward object constancy. The rapprochement crisis, with its mix of clinging and pushing away, is often linked to later difficulties with closeness and separateness.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Psychoanalytic therapy: object relations theory and Mahler's separation-individuation
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

552. nce-s-cou-180 · Human Growth and Development · psychodynamic and psychoanalytic theory · easy · In review

A 2-year-old insists on bringing a worn stuffed rabbit to child care and clutches it when her father leaves. In Winnicott's object relations theory, what function does this transitional object serve?
A. It signals an insecure attachment that will need professional treatment
Transitional objects are a normal part of development, not a sign of pathology.
B. It soothes her and bridges her move from union with a parent to separateness ✔ KEY
Winnicott saw the transitional object as an intermediate space that helps the child tolerate separation.
C. It reflects fixation at the oral stage caused by weaning that came too early
This applies Freud's psychosexual fixation, not Winnicott's concept.
D. It is a part-object she splits into all-good and all-bad parts to manage fear
Splitting and part-objects come from Melanie Klein, not the transitional object concept.
Rationale: Winnicott described the transitional object as the child's first "not-me" possession, standing between inner and outer reality and helping the child manage the gradual move to independence. It develops within a holding environment provided by a good-enough mother, who meets needs well at first and then fails in small, tolerable ways.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Psychoanalytic therapy: object relations (Winnicott, Klein)
⚑ Check: Confirm Corey's object-relations section names Winnicott's transitional object and good-enough mother.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

Core Counseling Attributes

48 items · NCE weight 8% (13 of 160 scored items)

553. nce-s-cor-001 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · empathy and its levels · medium · In review

A 34-year-old client says, "My boss praised my project in front of everyone, but then gave the promotion to someone else. I don't know what to think." Which counselor response is an interchangeable (Level 3) response on Carkhuff's empathy scale?
A. You should ask your boss directly why you were passed over this time.
Advice-giving ignores the client's feelings entirely; it is subtractive (Level 1 or 2), not interchangeable.
B. You feel confused because the praise and the promotion decision don't match. ✔ KEY
This captures the feeling (confusion) and its stated cause at the same depth the client expressed, which is the definition of a Level 3 interchangeable response.
C. Underneath the confusion, you may fear that your hard work goes unrecognized.
This goes beyond what the client expressed to an underlying feeling and meaning, making it additive (Level 4), not interchangeable.
D. Lots of people get passed over at work, and it usually works out fine in the end.
Reassurance minimizes the experience and shifts away from the client's feelings, a subtractive response.
Rationale: Carkhuff's scale rates counselor responses from 1 to 5. Level 3 is the minimally facilitative, interchangeable level: the counselor reflects essentially the same feeling and meaning the client expressed, adding nothing and taking nothing away. Levels 1 and 2 subtract from the client's message, and Levels 4 and 5 add depth beyond it.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Carkhuff's scale of empathic understanding, Levels 1-5
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

554. nce-s-cor-002 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · empathy and its levels · hard · In review

In a sixth session, a graduate student says, "I keep telling everyone I'm fine with moving home after graduation. My parents are happy, so I guess I should be too." Which counselor response BEST illustrates additive (Level 4) empathy?
A. So you're moving home after graduation, and your parents are pleased with it.
This paraphrases the content but omits feeling; it is at best Level 2, slightly subtractive.
B. You feel fine about moving home, since your parents are happy with the plan.
This repeats the client's surface statement and misses the doubt in "I guess I should be"; it does not add depth.
C. Why do you think your parents' happiness matters so much in this decision?
A why-question invites intellectualizing and does not communicate understanding of the feeling, so it is not an empathic response.
D. You sound unsure, as if your own wishes got set aside to keep your parents happy. ✔ KEY
This names the implicit ambivalence and the meaning beneath it (setting aside one's own wishes), adding accurately to what the client said: Level 4.
Rationale: Additive empathy (Carkhuff Levels 4-5) goes beyond the client's explicit words to reflect feelings and meanings the client implied but did not fully state, which helps the client explore at a deeper level. To be additive rather than inaccurate, the reflection must stay grounded in cues the client gave, such as the hedged "I guess I should be."
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Advanced (additive) empathy, Carkhuff Levels 4-5
⚑ Check: Option A is rated Level 2 in its rationale; raters may disagree on the exact level (it is clearly not additive).
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

555. nce-s-cor-003 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · empathy and its levels · easy · In review

On Carkhuff's five-level scale of empathic understanding, a counselor response rated at Level 1 or Level 2 is described as which of the following?
A. Subtractive, detracting from what the client expressed ✔ KEY
Levels 1 and 2 are subtractive: they ignore or only partly capture the client's feelings and meaning.
B. Interchangeable, matching the client's expressed feeling
Interchangeable, minimally facilitative responses are Level 3.
C. Additive, reflecting feelings below the client's words
Additive responses that reach underlying feelings are Levels 4 and 5.
D. Facilitative, the baseline goal for beginning counselors
Level 3 is the minimally facilitative baseline counselors aim to reach consistently; Levels 1-2 fall below it.
Rationale: Carkhuff's scale runs from Level 1 (the response ignores or contradicts the client's feelings) to Level 5 (the response adds significantly to the client's awareness). Levels 1-2 are subtractive, Level 3 is interchangeable and minimally facilitative, and Levels 4-5 are additive.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Carkhuff's scale of empathic understanding
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

556. nce-s-cor-004 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · empathy and its levels · easy · In review

A client tearfully describes the recent death of her dog. Which counselor response reflects empathy rather than sympathy?
A. I'm so sorry; I lost my own dog last year and I still cry about it sometimes too.
This shifts the focus to the counselor's own loss and expresses pity or shared distress, which is sympathy and self-disclosure, not empathy.
B. That is such a sad thing to go through, and I feel terrible for you today.
Feeling sorry for the client is sympathy; it conveys the counselor's feeling rather than understanding of the client's.
C. Losing her has left a real emptiness in your days, and the grief feels heavy. ✔ KEY
This communicates accurate understanding of the client's own experience from her frame of reference, which is empathy.
D. At least she had a long life with you, and you gave her a very good home.
"At least" reassurance minimizes the loss and moves away from the client's feelings.
Rationale: Empathy is understanding the client's world as if it were one's own, without losing the "as if" quality, and communicating that understanding back. Sympathy centers on the helper's own feelings of sorrow or pity for the client, which can shift the focus away from the client.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: accurate empathic understanding
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

557. nce-s-cor-005 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · unconditional positive regard · medium · In review

A 52-year-old client says, "I yelled at my teenage son last night and called him useless. I'm ashamed to even tell you." Which counselor response BEST demonstrates unconditional positive regard?
A. That was harsh, but I'm sure you are a good parent most of the time anyway.
Reassurance about being a "good parent" is conditional praise; it evaluates the client rather than accepting the client.
B. Calling him useless can do real damage, so let's plan what to say instead.
This jumps to evaluation and correction before the client feels accepted; it is not an expression of UPR.
C. It took courage to share that, and I'm glad you trusted me with it here. ✔ KEY
This accepts the client as a person, without approving or condemning the behavior, and values the client's openness, which is UPR.
D. Don't be ashamed, since all parents lose their temper and say things they regret.
Telling the client not to feel shame dismisses the feeling and normalizes too quickly; it is reassurance, not acceptance.
Rationale: Rogers described unconditional positive regard as a warm acceptance of the client as a person, without conditions of worth. UPR does not mean approving of every behavior; it means the client's worth is not contingent on what is disclosed, which lowers defensiveness and supports self-exploration.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: unconditional positive regard and acceptance
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

558. nce-s-cor-006 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · congruence and genuineness · medium · In review

Midway through a session, a client asks, "You look distracted. Are you even listening to me?" The counselor realizes her attention had drifted. Which response BEST demonstrates congruence?
A. You're right, my mind wandered for a moment. I'm with you now; please go on. ✔ KEY
The counselor's words match her inner experience, she owns it briefly, and she returns the focus to the client, which is congruence.
B. Of course I'm listening, and I have been following everything you've said.
Denying a lapse the counselor knows occurred is incongruent; outward words do not match inner experience.
C. It sounds like you worry people don't listen to you. Tell me more about that.
Reflecting the client's concern here deflects from the counselor's actual lapse and avoids genuineness.
D. I've had a long, stressful day with other clients, so I'm tired and distracted.
This is honest but over-discloses and shifts the focus to the counselor's needs rather than the relationship.
Rationale: Congruence (genuineness) means the counselor's outward behavior is consistent with inner experience, without a professional facade. Rogers viewed it as the most basic of the core conditions. Being genuine does not require disclosing every feeling; the counselor shares what is relevant to the relationship and keeps the focus on the client.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: congruence or genuineness
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

559. nce-s-cor-007 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · therapeutic alliance · easy · In review

Bordin's pantheoretical model of the working alliance consists of which three components?
A. Empathy, congruence, and positive regard
These are Rogers' core conditions, not Bordin's alliance components.
B. Rapport, insight, and corrective feedback
These are general therapy processes, not the components Bordin named.
C. Trust, transference, and client motivation
Transference is a psychodynamic concept; Bordin's model was explicitly pantheoretical.
D. Agreement on goals, tasks, and the bond ✔ KEY
Bordin defined the working alliance as agreement on goals, agreement on tasks, and the emotional bond between counselor and client.
Rationale: Bordin (1979) proposed that the working alliance has three parts: agreement on the goals of counseling, agreement on the tasks used to reach them, and the affective bond between counselor and client. Because it is pantheoretical, the model applies across approaches, and alliance strength is one of the most consistent predictors of outcome.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — The working alliance: goals, tasks, and bond
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

560. nce-s-cor-008 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · therapeutic alliance · hard · In review

In the fourth session, a client who has been completing CBT thought records says flatly, "I did the homework again, I guess. Whatever helps you." The client has arrived late twice. What should the counselor do FIRST?
A. Review the thought record in detail and praise the client for completing it
Proceeding with the task ignores the withdrawal cues and leaves a possible rupture unaddressed.
B. Invite the client to talk about how the work together is feeling so far ✔ KEY
Openly exploring the relationship addresses a likely withdrawal rupture and checks agreement on tasks and goals before continuing.
C. Set a lateness policy so that attendance does not continue to slip further
Focusing on rules treats the lateness as a compliance issue and can deepen the rupture.
D. Switch to a different intervention, since thought records are not working
Changing tasks unilaterally skips collaboration; the counselor does not yet know what the client wants or is reacting to.
Rationale: Flat compliance ("whatever helps you") and lateness suggest a withdrawal rupture in the alliance, often reflecting disagreement about tasks or goals or strain in the bond. Research on rupture and repair supports raising the relationship directly and nondefensively, which lets the counselor renegotiate tasks and goals collaboratively. Successfully repaired ruptures are associated with better outcomes.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Working alliance: goals, tasks, bond; addressing alliance ruptures
⚑ Check: Rupture-repair evidence (Safran et al.) is cited to a general Gladding alliance reference.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

561. nce-s-cor-009 · Social and Cultural Diversity · cultural humility · medium · In review

A counselor who has completed many multicultural trainings begins work with a Hmong American client. According to Hook and colleagues' model of cultural humility, which stance BEST reflects cultural humility?
A. Ask the client what their culture means to them and stay open to being corrected ✔ KEY
Cultural humility is an other-oriented, curious stance that treats the client as the expert on their own cultural identity.
B. Draw on prior training about Hmong customs to anticipate the client's values
Applying general group knowledge as a template risks stereotyping; it reflects a knowledge-based, not humble, stance.
C. Set cultural issues aside unless the client raises them first in the session
Waiting for the client to raise culture places the burden on the client and can signal that culture is unwelcome.
D. Treat the training already completed as sufficient competence for this client
Viewing competence as a finished achievement contradicts the ongoing, lifelong nature of humility.
Rationale: Hook et al. (2013) described cultural humility as an interpersonal stance that is other-oriented rather than self-focused, marked by respect, openness, and lack of superiority regarding the client's cultural background. It is an ongoing process of self-reflection rather than a fixed body of knowledge, and clients' perceptions of it are associated with a stronger alliance.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Cultural humility as an other-oriented stance
⚑ Check: Confirm the cited Sue & Sue edition discusses Hook et al.'s cultural humility model.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

562. nce-s-cor-010 · Social and Cultural Diversity · counselor self-awareness and bias · medium · In review

A counselor notices that she schedules a client who lives in public housing for shorter sessions and assigns fewer homework tasks, assuming the client "won't follow through." What is the MOST appropriate next step?
A. Refer the client to a counselor who has more experience with low-income clients
Referral based on the counselor's bias, rather than competence limits, abandons the client and avoids the counselor's own work.
B. Continue as planned, since shorter sessions may reduce the client's burden
This rationalizes the bias instead of examining it and keeps treating the client differently.
C. Examine the assumption in supervision and restore an equitable treatment plan ✔ KEY
Recognizing an implicit bias, exploring it in supervision, and correcting its effect on care reflects counselor self-awareness.
D. Tell the client about the bias so the client can decide whether to continue
Disclosing the bias burdens the client with the counselor's issue; the counselor should first address it through supervision.
Rationale: Counselor self-awareness of attitudes, beliefs, and biases is the first dimension of multicultural competence. Biases about social class can shape clinical decisions without conscious intent. When a counselor notices differential treatment, the ethical response is to examine it, often through supervision or consultation, and correct its effect on services.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Counselor awareness of own assumptions, values, and biases · ACA Code of Ethics — C.5 Nondiscrimination
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

563. nce-s-cor-011 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · countertransference · easy · In review

A counselor notices he feels unusually irritated and impatient with an older male client who reminds him of his own critical father. This reaction is BEST described as
A. transference by the client
Transference is the client's projection of past relationships onto the counselor; here the reaction is the counselor's.
B. countertransference ✔ KEY
The counselor's emotional reaction to the client, shaped by his own unresolved history, is countertransference.
C. resistance in the client
Resistance refers to client behavior that impedes change, not the counselor's feelings.
D. compassion fatigue
Compassion fatigue is cumulative exhaustion from trauma exposure, not a reaction tied to a specific personal history.
Rationale: Countertransference refers to the counselor's emotional reactions to a client, particularly those rooted in the counselor's own unresolved conflicts or past relationships. It is not inherently harmful, but unexamined countertransference can distort the counselor's perceptions and responses, so recognizing it is the first step to managing it.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Psychoanalytic therapy: transference and countertransference
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

564. nce-s-cor-012 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · countertransference · medium · In review

A counselor whose sister died by overdose finds herself giving extra session time and her personal cell number to a young adult client in early recovery. What is the BEST course of action?
A. Keep the extra contact, since it clearly helps the client stay engaged
This keeps a boundary crossing driven by the counselor's needs rather than the client's welfare.
B. Transfer the client right away to avoid any further personal reactions
Abrupt transfer is premature; countertransference can often be managed and abrupt referral may harm the client.
C. Disclose the sister's death so the client understands her strong concern
This self-disclosure serves the counselor's needs and burdens the client.
D. Seek supervision on the reaction and restore usual session boundaries ✔ KEY
Recognizing the countertransference, processing it in supervision, and restoring boundaries protects the client and the work.
Rationale: Countertransference can show up as overinvolvement, rescuing, or boundary crossings that meet the counselor's needs. Effective management involves self-awareness, supervision or personal counseling, and returning to boundaries that serve the client. Referral is reserved for cases where the counselor cannot remain objective after these steps.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Countertransference and the counselor as a person · ACA Code of Ethics — A.6.b Extending Conventional Boundaries
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

565. nce-s-cor-013 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · countertransference · hard · In review

A supervisor tells a trainee, "Every feeling you have toward a client, not just the conflicts from your own past, can be useful information about the client and the relationship." This statement reflects which view of countertransference?
A. Classical view, treating it as an obstacle to be eliminated
The classical (Freudian) view limits countertransference to the counselor's unresolved conflicts and treats it as interference.
B. Behavioral view, treating it as a learned response to extinguish
Countertransference is not framed as a conditioned response in behavioral theory; this distractor misattributes the concept.
C. Complementary view, limited to the client's projected roles
The complementary conception frames countertransference as the counselor's reaction to the interpersonal pull of the client's style, a narrower idea than all feelings toward the client.
D. Totalistic view, including all counselor reactions to clients ✔ KEY
The totalistic view defines countertransference as all of the counselor's emotional reactions and sees them as potentially useful data.
Rationale: The classical view, rooted in Freud, defines countertransference narrowly as the counselor's unconscious, conflict-based reactions to the client's transference and treats it as an impediment. The totalistic view broadens it to all of the counselor's emotional responses and treats them as a source of understanding. Contemporary integrative views keep the focus on conflict-based reactions while stressing that, once understood, they can inform the work.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Psychoanalytic therapy: countertransference and its therapeutic use
⚑ Check: Classical/totalistic/complementary views come from Gelso & Hayes; confirm Corey covers the totalistic view or swap the source.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

566. nce-s-cor-014 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · nonjudgmental stance · medium · In review

A college student says, "I've been hooking up with different people most weekends, and my roommate thinks I'm a mess." Which counselor response BEST reflects a nonjudgmental stance?
A. Your roommate may have a point, so let's look at the risks you're taking.
Siding with the roommate conveys the counselor's judgment before understanding the client's view.
B. Your roommate sees it one way. I'm curious how you feel about these weekends. ✔ KEY
This neither condemns nor endorses the behavior and invites the client's own perspective, which is nonjudgmental.
C. There's nothing wrong with that at all, and your roommate should not judge you.
Approval is also an evaluation; it imposes the counselor's values in the opposite direction.
D. What do you think is missing in your life that leads you to keep doing this?
This presumes the behavior signals a deficit, a judgment embedded in the question.
Rationale: A nonjudgmental stance means the counselor suspends both disapproval and approval and seeks to understand the client's experience from the client's frame of reference. Counselors avoid imposing their own values on clients, which allows clients to explore their choices without becoming defensive.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

567. nce-s-cor-015 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · warmth and respect · easy · In review

A 70-year-old widower arrives early for his first session and seems nervous. Which counselor behavior BEST conveys warmth and respect?
A. Greet him by name, ask how he prefers to be addressed, and offer him a seat ✔ KEY
This shows genuine interest and respects his preferences and dignity, communicating warmth and respect.
B. Call him "sweetie" and speak slowly and loudly so he can follow along easily
Endearments and exaggerated speech are elderspeak; they are patronizing and disrespectful.
C. Hand him the intake forms and ask him to wait until his appointment time
This is procedural and distant, and it ignores his visible nervousness.
D. Tell him there is no need to be nervous because most clients feel fine later
This dismisses his feelings and offers reassurance in place of attunement.
Rationale: Warmth is conveyed through friendly, caring verbal and nonverbal behavior, and respect is shown by treating the client as a capable person with preferences and dignity. Asking how a client wishes to be addressed is a simple, culturally responsive way to communicate both, and avoiding ageist communication such as elderspeak is part of respect.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Building a counseling relationship: warmth and respect
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

568. nce-s-cor-016 · Social and Cultural Diversity · awareness of power and privilege in the counseling relationship · medium · In review

A White counselor working with a Black client hears the client say, "I wasn't sure I could talk about racism at work with you." Which counselor response BEST shows awareness of power and privilege in the relationship?
A. I don't really see color, so you can talk to me about anything you need to here.
Color-blind statements deny the relevance of race and the client's concern, which is a microinvalidation.
B. I've had many Black clients, so I understand a lot about what you face at work.
Claiming understanding based on experience with other clients overstates the counselor's knowledge and dismisses the concern.
C. As a White counselor I may miss things, and I'd like to hear it if you're willing. ✔ KEY
This names the racial difference and the limits of the counselor's perspective, and invites the client's experience without pressure.
D. Let's focus on what you can control at work, since we can't change the people there.
Redirecting away from racism minimizes a systemic experience and avoids the topic the client raised.
Rationale: Counselors from privileged groups hold both professional and social power. Broaching racial and cultural differences directly and nondefensively, and acknowledging the limits of one's own perspective, signals that the client's experiences of oppression are welcome. Color-blind or minimizing responses are common microaggressions that weaken trust.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Power, privilege, and microaggressions in counseling; color-blindness
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

569. nce-s-cor-017 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · empathy and its levels · medium · In review

A 41-year-old man ordered to counseling after a road-rage incident sits down and says, "This is a joke. The other guy cut me off and I'm the one stuck here wasting my Thursday." Which counselor response BEST conveys empathy?
A. The court decided you need to be here, so let's make good use of the hour today.
This sides with the court and moves to the agenda without acknowledging the client's feelings, a subtractive response.
B. Getting angry on the road is risky, and that is what we need to look at together.
This confronts the behavior before the client feels heard, which tends to increase defensiveness in a mandated client.
C. You're frustrated, because it feels unfair that you're the one paying the price. ✔ KEY
This accurately reflects the feeling (frustration) and its meaning (unfairness) from the client's frame of reference without agreeing or arguing.
D. I hear that, but many people find these sessions useful once they give them a try.
"I hear that, but" discounts the feeling and shifts to persuasion, which is reassurance rather than empathy.
Rationale: Empathy with an angry or mandated client means communicating understanding of the client's feelings and perspective, not defending the referral source or confronting the behavior first. An accurate reflection lowers defensiveness and builds the alliance needed for later work on the behavior that led to the referral.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Empathy and working with reluctant or resistant clients
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

570. nce-s-cor-018 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · empathy and its levels · hard · In review

A client says, "My sister borrowed money again and didn't pay it back. She's completely selfish, and anyone in my place would cut her off for good." Which counselor response communicates empathy WITHOUT signaling agreement with the client's judgment?
A. You feel hurt and fed up, and cutting her off seems like the only way to stop it. ✔ KEY
This reflects the client's feelings and how the situation looks to the client, conveying understanding without endorsing the conclusion that the sister is selfish.
B. She does sound selfish, and you'd be right to protect yourself from her by now.
This agrees with the client's evaluation of the sister, confusing empathy with agreement and taking sides.
C. Maybe your sister is struggling in ways that you might not know about yet, though.
Offering the sister's side challenges the client prematurely and communicates that the counselor does not understand the client.
D. Cutting off family is a big step, so let's think carefully before you decide.
This shifts to cautionary advice and skips reflecting the client's feelings, so it is not an empathic response.
Rationale: Empathy is understanding the client's world "as if" it were one's own while keeping the "as if" quality. It reflects the client's feelings and perceptions as the client experiences them; it neither agrees with nor disputes the client's judgments. Distinguishing empathy from agreement lets the counselor stay with the client without becoming an ally against third parties.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: accurate empathic understanding and the "as if" quality
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

571. nce-s-cor-019 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · unconditional positive regard · medium · In review

A 29-year-old client who left a stable nursing job to work as a touring musician says she is happy with the choice, though money is tight. The counselor privately thinks the decision is unwise. Which approach BEST reflects unconditional positive regard and respect for client autonomy?
A. Point out the financial risks so the client can reconsider before it is too late
Steering the client toward the counselor's preferred choice imposes the counselor's values on a decision the client has not asked to revisit.
B. Accept her choice as hers to make and explore the goals she brings to counseling ✔ KEY
Valuing the client without conditions and following her own goals honors UPR and self-determination, even when the counselor would choose differently.
C. Praise the decision warmly so the client feels supported in following her dream
Praise is an evaluation too; UPR is acceptance of the person, not approval of choices, and the praise would be incongruent with the counselor's view.
D. Share the honest concern about the career change since genuineness matters most
Genuineness does not require voicing every personal opinion; volunteering disapproval of a lawful life choice imposes values.
Rationale: Unconditional positive regard means prizing the client as a person regardless of whether the counselor agrees with the client's choices. Combined with respect for self-determination, it means counselors do not impose personal values on clients' lawful life decisions and instead work on the goals clients bring.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: unconditional positive regard and acceptance · ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

572. nce-s-cor-020 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · unconditional positive regard · easy · In review

Rogers held that when a counselor provides unconditional positive regard, empathy, and congruence, clients move toward growth because of an innate drive to develop their capacities. He called this drive the
A. striving for superiority
Striving for superiority (or significance) is Adler's concept of the movement toward overcoming felt inferiority.
B. will to meaning
The will to meaning is Frankl's existential concept, central to logotherapy.
C. hierarchy of needs
The hierarchy of needs is Maslow's model of motivation, not Rogers' term for the growth drive.
D. actualizing tendency ✔ KEY
Rogers described the actualizing tendency as the organism's inherent tendency to develop its capacities in ways that maintain and enhance it.
Rationale: Person-centered theory rests on trust in the actualizing tendency, an inborn movement toward growth and fulfillment. The counselor does not direct change; instead, the core conditions create a climate in which the client's own actualizing tendency can operate and conditions of worth lose their hold.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: the actualizing tendency
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

573. nce-s-cor-021 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · congruence and genuineness · medium · In review

A client describes years of failed fertility treatments. The counselor went through a similar loss and feels a wave of sadness. Which response BEST reflects genuineness and intentional use of self without inappropriate self-disclosure?
A. I'm moved hearing how much hope and heartbreak these years have held for you. ✔ KEY
The counselor shares an authentic, here-and-now reaction that is relevant to the client and keeps the focus on the client's experience.
B. I went through fertility treatments too, so I know exactly how painful this is.
This disclosure shifts focus to the counselor and claims identical experience, which can silence the client's own version of the loss.
C. Let's look at the coping strategies that have helped you through these years.
Moving straight to coping sidesteps the emotion in the room; the counselor masks her reaction rather than using it.
D. Many couples face this, and there are other paths to parenthood worth exploring.
Normalizing and problem-solving prematurely minimizes the grief and does not reflect a genuine, attuned response.
Rationale: Congruence means the counselor's outward expression matches inner experience, without a professional facade. Genuineness does not require telling one's personal history; intentional use of self means sharing reactions only when they serve the client. Disclosures of the counselor's own life should be brief, purposeful, and returned quickly to the client.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — Person-centered therapy: congruence; therapist self-disclosure
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

574. nce-s-cor-022 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · congruence and genuineness · easy · In review

During a video session, a client says, "On this screen it's hard to tell whether what I say really lands with you." Which counselor adjustment BEST supports genuineness in telehealth?
A. Ask more questions so the client can see the counselor is paying close attention
More questions do not convey the counselor's reactions and may feel like an interview rather than a genuine relationship.
B. Reassure the client that the counselor is listening carefully even if it is hard to see
Reassurance asks the client to trust without changing anything about how the counselor's presence comes across.
C. Put more reactions into words, since the camera filters out many nonverbal cues ✔ KEY
Verbalizing reactions compensates for the reduced nonverbal channel so the client can experience the counselor as present and authentic.
D. Suggest switching to phone sessions so that video issues stop being a distraction
Phone sessions remove even more nonverbal information and avoid the client's concern rather than addressing it.
Rationale: Video sessions reduce the nonverbal cues, such as posture, small facial changes, and eye contact, that usually convey a counselor's presence. To remain genuine and transparent, counselors can name their reactions more explicitly, look toward the camera, and check in about how the connection feels to the client.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Genuineness; technology and distance counseling
⚑ Check: Telehealth genuineness guidance is general practice wisdom; confirm the cited Gladding chapter addresses technology-assisted counseling or swap the source.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

575. nce-s-cor-023 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · therapeutic alliance · medium · In review

A 15-year-old brought to counseling by his mother crosses his arms and says, "She's the one who wanted this. I don't have anything to talk about." Which counselor response is MOST likely to begin building a working alliance?
A. Your mom is really worried about you, so it would help to tell me what has been going on.
This aligns the counselor with the parent's agenda and pressures the teen, weakening the bond.
B. Coming here wasn't your idea. I'm curious if anything would make this worth it to you. ✔ KEY
This acknowledges the teen's lack of choice and invites his own goals, building agreement on goals and the bond.
C. That's fine. We can just sit quietly until you decide you're ready to start talking.
Passive waiting leaves the teen without a reason to engage and does nothing to establish shared goals.
D. Most teens feel that way at first, but they usually end up liking counseling a lot.
Generalized reassurance dismisses his stated position and can sound like the counselor is selling something.
Rationale: Adolescents brought by parents often arrive reluctant. The alliance grows when the counselor acknowledges the teen's autonomy, separates from the parent's agenda, and invites the teen to name goals of his own. In Bordin's terms, this begins building agreement on goals and the bond.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Working alliance with reluctant clients and adolescents
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

576. nce-s-cor-024 · Social and Cultural Diversity · awareness of power and privilege in the counseling relationship · hard · In review

A court-mandated client on probation asks at intake, "So whatever I say in here goes straight to my probation officer, right?" The client has signed a release limited to attendance and progress reports. What is the BEST response?
A. Reassure the client that sessions are confidential so that he will speak more freely
Promising full confidentiality is inaccurate given the signed release and would undermine trust when reports are sent.
B. Tell the client that the probation officer will decide what is shared from sessions
The scope of disclosure is set by the release and law, not by the officer; this also cedes the client's informed role.
C. Suggest that the client avoid sharing anything that could get him into legal trouble
This advises concealment and undermines the purpose of counseling instead of clarifying the actual limits.
D. Explain exactly what the release permits to be shared and invite questions about it ✔ KEY
Transparent, specific information about the limits of confidentiality acknowledges the power imbalance and supports informed participation.
Rationale: Mandated clients face a real power imbalance: the counselor reports to a system that holds consequences over them. Counselors address this by explaining clearly, at the start and as needed, what will and will not be disclosed and to whom. Honest transparency about the counselor's dual accountability is the foundation for trust in mandated work.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — B.1.d Explanation of Limitations
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

577. nce-s-cor-025 · Social and Cultural Diversity · cultural humility · medium · In review

In a first session, a counselor told a U.S.-born Korean American client, "Your English is excellent." The client became quiet for the rest of the hour. At the next session, what should the counselor do FIRST?
A. Wait to see whether the client brings up the comment before addressing it in session
Waiting puts the burden of raising the harm on the client and lets the rupture persist.
B. Explain that the remark was meant as a compliment and was not intended to offend
Defending intent centers the counselor and minimizes the impact on the client.
C. Name the comment, take responsibility for its impact, and invite the client's view ✔ KEY
Nondefensively acknowledging a microaggression and inviting the client's experience is the core of rupture repair with cultural humility.
D. Focus on the presenting problem so the session is not sidetracked by the earlier slip
Moving on avoids the rupture; unaddressed microaggressions are linked to weaker alliances and dropout.
Rationale: Remarks that assume an Asian American is a foreigner ("alien in one's own land") are a recognized microaggression. When a counselor commits one, cultural humility calls for owning the impact rather than defending intent, and openly inviting the client's reaction. Repairing such ruptures can strengthen the relationship.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Racial microaggressions: alien in one's own land
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

578. nce-s-cor-026 · Social and Cultural Diversity · cultural humility · hard · In review

A second-generation Nigerian American counselor begins working with a 24-year-old woman who immigrated from Nigeria two years ago. The counselor thinks, "I grew up with this, so I already know what her parents expect of her." Which stance BEST reflects cultural humility?
A. Draw on shared heritage to explain the family expectations the client is facing
Using one's own background as a template assumes sameness and replaces the client's account with the counselor's.
B. Ask how she sees her family's expectations and stay open to differences from her own ✔ KEY
This treats the client as the expert on her experience and stays alert to differences in generation, region, ethnicity, and immigration history.
C. Refer her to a counselor of another culture to avoid any bias from the shared heritage
A shared background is not grounds for referral; the task is to examine assumptions, not avoid the client.
D. Disclose the shared background early so the client knows she will be understood
Promising understanding on the basis of shared heritage reinforces the assumption of sameness.
Rationale: Cultural humility applies even when counselor and client share a cultural background. Within-group differences in generation, acculturation, region, language, religion, and personal values can be large, and assuming sameness can lead to blind spots or overidentification. A humble, curious stance invites the client to define what her culture means to her.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Within-group differences and the dangers of assumed similarity
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

579. nce-s-cor-027 · Social and Cultural Diversity · counselor self-awareness and bias · medium · In review

A counselor with strong religious convictions works with a client who wants help deciding whether to leave her faith community. The counselor notices a pull to encourage the client to stay. What is the MOST appropriate action?
A. Refer the client elsewhere, because the counselor's beliefs conflict with the goal
The ACA Code bars referral based solely on the counselor's personal values; the counselor must first work to bracket them.
B. Share the counselor's own beliefs openly so the client can weigh them in deciding
Offering personal religious views on the client's decision imposes the counselor's values.
C. Gently point out what the client may lose by leaving her supportive community
Emphasizing losses of only one option steers the client toward the counselor's preference.
D. Seek consultation, set aside personal views, and follow the client's own process ✔ KEY
Recognizing the pull, getting consultation, and keeping the focus on the client's goals reflect self-awareness and A.4.b.
Rationale: Self-awareness includes noticing when personal religious or political values press on clinical work. The ACA Code directs counselors to be aware of their own values and avoid imposing them, seeking training where they are at risk of doing so, and it prohibits referral based solely on the counselor's personal values.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values · ACA Code of Ethics — A.11.b Values Within Termination and Referral
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

580. nce-s-cor-028 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · countertransference · easy · In review

A counselor whose parents had a bitter divorce works with a 16-year-old caught in a custody dispute. She finds herself angry at the client's father and urging the teen to "stand up to him." This pattern is BEST described as
A. overidentification ✔ KEY
The counselor is merging her own history with the client's, losing objectivity and taking sides, a form of countertransference.
B. parallel process
Parallel process refers to dynamics in counseling being replicated in supervision, or the reverse.
C. advocacy
Advocacy addresses systemic barriers on behalf of a client; it is not driven by the counselor's unresolved personal history.
D. client transference
Transference is the client's projection onto the counselor; here the reaction originates in the counselor.
Rationale: Overidentification occurs when a counselor sees the client's situation through the lens of his or her own experience, losing the "as if" boundary of empathy. It is a common form of countertransference that can lead the counselor to take sides or push the client toward choices the counselor wished for, so it calls for self-reflection and supervision.
References: Corey (Theory & Practice) — The counselor as a person: countertransference and overidentification
⚑ Check: Confirm Corey (Theory & Practice) discusses overidentification by name; Corey's Issues & Ethics may be the better home for it.
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

581. nce-s-cor-029 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · nonjudgmental stance · easy · In review

A client says, "I still smoke weed most nights to fall asleep. Go ahead and give me the lecture." Which counselor response BEST reflects a nonjudgmental stance?
A. No lecture. I'd like to understand what it does for you and how it's working. ✔ KEY
This sets aside evaluation and invites the client's own view of benefits and costs, a nonjudgmental and collaborative stance.
B. I won't lecture, but you know nightly use can make your sleep worse over time.
The "but" delivers the lecture anyway, conveying judgment and likely increasing defensiveness.
C. It sounds like you already know it's a problem, or you wouldn't expect a lecture.
This interprets the comment as an admission of a problem, imposing the counselor's conclusion.
D. Lots of people use cannabis for sleep now, so it isn't a big concern for me.
Dismissing the topic is approval, another kind of judgment, and closes off exploration.
Rationale: A nonjudgmental stance suspends both disapproval and approval in favor of curiosity about the client's experience. With substance use, exploring what the substance does for the client and how it is working invites honest self-evaluation and is consistent with motivational interviewing's spirit of acceptance.
References: Miller & Rollnick (MI) — Spirit of MI: acceptance (absolute worth, autonomy support)
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

582. nce-s-cor-030 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · nonjudgmental stance · medium · In review

A 33-year-old single mother mentions in passing that she does sex work to pay her bills, then says she came to counseling because of anxiety about her son's problems at school. What should the counselor do?
A. Shift the focus to her work, since it is likely the underlying source of her anxiety
Assuming the work is the real problem overrides the client's stated goal and reflects the counselor's judgment.
B. Follow her stated concern while leaving room to discuss work or safety if she wishes ✔ KEY
Respecting the client's agenda without ignoring possible safety needs reflects a nonjudgmental, client-centered stance.
C. Give her referrals for job training so she has other options to support her family
Unrequested job referrals imply her work must change, imposing values she did not ask the counselor to apply.
D. Avoid any mention of her work so that she does not feel judged in this session
Treating the topic as unspeakable can also signal judgment and may miss safety concerns she wants to raise.
Rationale: A nonjudgmental stance means the counselor does not treat a stigmatized behavior as the presumed problem. The client sets the agenda, and the counselor stays open to discussing work, health, or safety when the client chooses, without pathologizing or avoiding the topic.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

583. nce-s-cor-031 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · warmth and respect · easy · In review

A client arrives sobbing and breathing rapidly after learning she is being evicted at the end of the week. Which counselor response BEST conveys warmth in this moment?
A. Hand her a list of housing resources so she can start making calls right away
Resources may help later, but moving to tasks while she is flooded ignores her emotional state.
B. Ask her to describe the eviction notice in detail to see what her options are
Detailed fact-gathering before she is calmer is task-focused and can add to her distress.
C. Tell her firmly that panicking will not help and that she needs to calm down
A directive to stop panicking is cold and dismissive, and it rarely reduces distress.
D. Sit with her, speak in a calm, steady voice, and acknowledge how scared she is ✔ KEY
A calm, caring presence and acknowledgment of her fear communicate warmth and help her regulate before problem-solving.
Rationale: Warmth is communicated largely through nonverbal behavior, including tone of voice, pacing, and attentive presence, together with acknowledgment of the client's feelings. In acute distress, a warm and steady presence helps the client regulate enough to engage in the practical problem-solving that follows.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Warmth and nonverbal communication in the helping relationship
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

584. nce-s-cor-032 · Social and Cultural Diversity · awareness of power and privilege in the counseling relationship · medium · In review

A counselor is meeting with a Spanish-speaking client through a trained professional interpreter. Which practice BEST preserves the client's voice and respects the counseling relationship?
A. Ask the interpreter to summarize what the client says to keep sessions brief
Summaries filter the client's words through the interpreter and lose emotional content.
B. Ask the client's bilingual teenage son to interpret, since the family trusts him
Family members, especially children, compromise accuracy and confidentiality and shift family power roles.
C. Speak directly to the client in the first person rather than to the interpreter ✔ KEY
Addressing the client directly keeps her at the center of the relationship and the interpreter in a conduit role.
D. Speak with the interpreter after sessions to learn the cultural meaning of her words
Relying on the interpreter as cultural expert behind the client's back can sideline her own account of her experience.
Rationale: Interpreted sessions add a third person and can shift power away from the client. Best practice is to use a trained interpreter rather than family, brief the interpreter beforehand, and speak directly to the client in the first person so that the relationship remains between counselor and client.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.2.c Developmental and Cultural Sensitivity · Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Language barriers and use of interpreters
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

585. nce-s-cor-033 · Social and Cultural Diversity · counselor self-awareness and bias · medium · In review

A counselor who sincerely holds egalitarian values reviews her recorded sessions for supervision. She notices that with her Latino clients she offers fewer reflections, interrupts more often, and moves to advice sooner than with her White clients. She had not been aware of the difference. This pattern BEST illustrates
A. implicit bias operating outside her conscious awareness ✔ KEY
Automatic, unintended differences in behavior toward a group, despite consciously held egalitarian beliefs, are the hallmark of implicit (unconscious) bias.
B. explicit prejudice that she consciously holds but conceals
Explicit prejudice is consciously endorsed. The counselor sincerely holds egalitarian values and was unaware of the pattern.
C. cultural encapsulation produced by a narrow training program
Wrenn's cultural encapsulation describes defining reality through one's own cultural lens. It does not specifically explain unaware, group-specific differences in her microskills.
D. countertransference rooted in conflicts from her own family
Countertransference stems from the counselor's personal history with significant others. Nothing suggests a family conflict; the pattern tracks client ethnicity.
Rationale: Implicit bias refers to attitudes and associations that operate automatically and outside awareness, so well-intentioned counselors can treat groups differently without meaning to. Sue and Sue stress that good intentions do not protect against unintentional bias; recorded sessions, supervision and ongoing self-examination are how counselors detect it.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Implicit bias and unintentional racism in well-intentioned helping professionals
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

586. nce-s-cor-034 · Social and Cultural Diversity · counselor self-awareness and bias · medium · In review

A 47-year-old client in a larger body seeks counseling for grief after his mother's death. He has not raised any concern about his weight. Over three sessions, the counselor finds herself suggesting exercise plans and asking about his eating. Which action BEST reflects counselor self-awareness?
A. Add a weight-loss goal to the plan, since weight affects mood and grief
This imposes the counselor's agenda on a client who came for grief and acts on the bias rather than examining it.
B. Notice her assumptions about his weight and refocus on the grief he brought ✔ KEY
Recognizing the counselor-driven assumption and returning to the client's own goal is self-aware, client-centered practice consistent with ACA A.4.b.
C. Refer him to a dietitian so his eating habits can be addressed by an expert
A referral the client did not request still acts on the counselor's assumption about his body rather than on his presenting concern.
D. Ask him directly whether his weight played a part in his mother's death
This question extends the counselor's weight focus into his grief and may shame him; it reflects the bias rather than awareness of it.
Rationale: Self-awareness means noticing when personal values or assumptions, including those about body size, are steering the work. ACA Standard A.4.b directs counselors to avoid imposing their own values and to respect the client's goals. The counselor should examine where the weight focus came from and return to the grief the client brought.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values · Corey (Theory & Practice) — The counselor as a person: self-awareness and personal values
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

587. nce-s-cor-035 · Social and Cultural Diversity · counselor self-awareness and bias · hard · In review

The week after a national election, a client spends several minutes praising a candidate the counselor strongly opposes. The counselor notices her jaw tightening. The client then asks, "You agree with me, right?" Which counselor response BEST reflects self-aware, ethical practice?
A. Honestly, I see it differently, but I respect your right to your own view.
Sharing political disagreement shifts focus to the counselor and risks imposing values; congruence does not require disclosing every opinion.
B. I do. A lot of people feel that way, so I can see why you are hopeful now.
Feigning agreement is incongruent and also brings the counselor's supposed politics into the session.
C. I keep my politics out of here, but I want to hear what this means for you. ✔ KEY
This gently declines to disclose, keeps the focus on the client, and invites exploration, which manages the counselor's reaction without acting on it.
D. Since we differ on this, another counselor might be a better fit for you.
ACA A.11.b cautions against referral based solely on the counselor's personal values; a political difference is not grounds for referral.
Rationale: Counselors are expected to notice their own value reactions, including political ones, and keep them from steering the session (ACA A.4.b). Self-disclosure of opinions should serve the client, and a politically charged question is usually best met by declining warmly and exploring its meaning for the client. Referral solely because of a values difference is discouraged under A.11.b.
References: ACA Code of Ethics — A.4.b Personal Values · ACA Code of Ethics — A.11.b Values Within Termination and Referral
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

588. nce-s-cor-036 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · warmth and respect · easy · In review

At a community mental health center, a 36-year-old client referred by his caseworker glares at the counselor and says, "You're just another paid stranger. You don't actually care what happens to me." Which counselor response BEST conveys warmth and respect?
A. I have years of training, so you can trust that I know how to help you.
Defending credentials centers the counselor and argues with the client's experience rather than respecting it.
B. I can't work with you if you speak to me in that tone during sessions.
The client is distrustful, not abusive. An early limit on tone reads as punitive and confirms his expectation that no one cares.
C. Let's set that aside and get through the intake questions for today.
Ignoring the statement dismisses the client's concern and treats him as paperwork, the opposite of respect.
D. Sounds like people haven't earned your trust. I'd like to, at your pace. ✔ KEY
This reflects the meaning behind the hostility without defensiveness and communicates a respectful wish to earn trust over time.
Rationale: Warmth and respect are tested most when a client is hostile. A nondefensive response that reflects the client's distrust, treats it as understandable, and leaves the client in control of the pace communicates care. Defending oneself, setting premature limits, or ignoring the comment tend to confirm the client's expectations.
References: Gladding (Counseling: A Comprehensive Profession) — Warmth, respect and working with reluctant or resistant clients
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

589. nce-s-cor-037 · Social and Cultural Diversity · warmth and respect · medium · In review

A 60-year-old Vietnamese immigrant father comes to counseling about conflict with his teenage son. In the first session he says, "You are the expert. Please tell me what I should do." Which counselor approach BEST combines respect with responsiveness to his request?
A. Offer some concrete suggestions and structure, checking how each idea fits his family ✔ KEY
Honoring his expectation of an active, expert helper while asking how ideas fit his family respects both his cultural frame and his autonomy.
B. Explain that counselors do not give advice and that he must find his own answers
A strictly nondirective stance may be experienced as unhelpful or as a lack of competence, and it dismisses his stated preference.
C. Tell him exactly what rules to set for his son, since he asked for clear direction
Directing without his input ignores his knowledge of his own family and values; structure should still be collaborative.
D. Ask him to first explore his deeper feelings about his son before any guidance
Insisting on emotional exploration before addressing his practical request disregards what he came for and may lead to early dropout.
Rationale: Sue and Sue note that many clients, especially those from cultures that value hierarchy and practical help, expect the counselor to take an active, directive role, and that a purely nondirective style can lead to early termination. Respect means meeting the client's expectations with structure and concrete input while still checking that suggestions fit the client's values.
References: Sue & Sue (Counseling the Culturally Diverse) — Culturally appropriate helping styles: directive versus nondirective approaches
☐ Approve☐ Revise☐ RetireNotes:

590. nce-s-cor-038 · Counseling and Helping Relationships · warmth and respect · easy · In review

A 38-year-old Army veteran referred for military sexual trauma tells the counselor in her second session, "I'm not ready to talk about what happened. I don't know if I ever will be." Which counselor response BEST respects the client's pace?
A. Avoiding it keeps symptoms going, so let's try to cover the details today.
Pressing for details before the client consents overrides her choice and can feel retraumatizing.
B. That's okay. You decide what we talk about and when, and we can go slowly. ✔ KEY
This affirms her control over disclosure, a core trauma-informed principle, and conveys respect for her readiness.
C. Could you give me just a short outline so I know what we're working with?
Asking for an outline right after she declines still pressures disclosure and disregards her stated limit.
D. Unless you talk about it, I'm not sure that counseling can help you much.
Making help conditional on disclosure is coercive and undermines safety and trust.
Rationale: Respecting a client's pace is especially important with trauma survivors. SAMHSA's trauma-informed principles emphasize safety, trustworthiness, and client voice and choice; counselors let clients control when and how much they disclose, building stabilization and trust first.
